2. P6C-MCP-01 — P2: complete the MCP proxy error result

Location: source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:660. Cases: MCP09 upstream-expired and upstream-wrong-audience. Both recover the response at lab-mcp09:proxy-upstream-error-recover, zero-based event 49, displayed step 50.

The corrected proxy properly retains downstream acceptance, reports the failed upstream grant and returns an HTTP 200 tool execution error. However, its JSON-RPC result contains isError and content without resultType. The selected MCP 2026-07-28 sender profile requires that field. Its tool-error example uses "complete" alongside isError: true.

result: {
  resultType: 'complete',
  isError: true,
  content: [/* preserve the existing upstream recovery explanation */]
}

Acceptance: both affected recovered bodies must contain resultType:'complete', isError:true and the matching downstream request ID. Downstream acceptance stays true, upstream acceptance stays false, protected output stays unavailable, and neither token appears in the returned body. Preserve HTTP 200 and the upstream-only recovery instruction. The independent scan found 22 recovered result bodies across the 117 MCP cases; these two are the only missing-field results.

The dated specification also tells receivers to default an absent field to complete for older-server compatibility. Consequently this is a current-profile sender conformance issue, not a claim of universal receiver rejection. It does not reopen the accepted P6-MCP-A1 actor/verdict correction.

Primary basis: MCP 2026-07-28 Base Overview — Result Responses / ResultType and Tools — Error Handling. Both were independently opened during this review. The small executable reproduction is included below.

P6-NFS-01 — closed: GETFH and result provenance

Relevant current source: src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 243–269.

All 28 reachable successful v4 OPEN requests now place GETFH immediately after OPEN in the same COMPOUND. OPEN creates only its stateid result and updates the modeled server CURRENT_FH; the following getfh-server creates the returned filehandle. The response explicitly associates the stateid with OPEN and the filehandle with GETFH. The client receives only the selected protected or untrusted wire representation, gains the decoded handle at receiver verification, and installs the current handle at open-accept.

The NFS01/default trace now exposes these boundaries:

Stage Zero-based event Journey step
namespace-open 46 47
open-server 54 55
getfh-server 55 56
open-response 58 59
open-response-verify 59 60
open-accept 60 61

The response's RPC XID and GSS sequence match its request. v4.0 retains its distinct OPEN_CONFIRM path, with a new explicit construction event consuming the verified GETFH handle and provisional stateid. v4.1+ retains SEQUENCE. Both NFS07 successful SECINFO variants preserve the consumed-current-filehandle distinction and restore the parent through PUTFH before LOOKUP/OPEN/GETFH. NFS03/NFS04 retain v3 LOOKUP and do not acquire invented v4 GETFH operations.

This closes the original operation/result error and its custody consequences. The relevant normative boundaries are RFC 8881, §§18.8 and 18.16.4.1, and RFC 7530, §16.16.4. The RFCs require GETFH after OPEN in the same COMPOUND; the corrected trace now expresses that relationship.

P6-NFS-02 — closed: post-Finished alert key lineage

Relevant current source: src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 105–117 and 466–489.

The server and client now each create a local master-secret state from their own handshake-secret state, followed by local directional application traffic secrets derived with the transcript through server Finished. Those operations occur before the client-certificate and host-policy denials. The alert creator uses the server-owned S2C secret; the client uses its own matching S2C copy to decrypt the received alert. Client plaintext alert custody starts at that decryption boundary.

Independently checked cases:

  • NFS11: missing-client-certificate, host-unauthorized, corrupt-application-record.
  • NFS12: missing-client-identity, invalid-client-identity, revoked-client.

For NFS12/missing-client-identity, the current zero-based event positions are server handshake flight creation 12, server/client master derivation 17/18, server/client application-secret derivation 19/20, alert encryption 26, wire receipt 27 and client decryption 28. This sequence makes the previously missing prerequisites observable.

All six paths keep keys local: no key artifact is sent in a message, and an endpoint never acquires the other endpoint's directional key copy. After failure, all ten modeled connection-temporary ephemeral, handshake, master and application-key artifacts are released, while long-term client/server private-key holdings remain. No case dispatches a file operation or yields file bytes. The five handshake-admission failures never mark either transport endpoint admitted. The corrupt-application-record case correctly has an earlier established connection, then closes it on record failure; the review does not incorrectly require its earlier acceptance to be false.

These checks close the missing key/operation provenance finding. RFC 9846, §4.5.3 specifies application-key protection for records after Finished, including server alerts responding to client certificate messages; §7.1 defines the master-secret and application-traffic derivation. The implementation remains a symbolic key-schedule lesson, not executed TLS cryptography.

P6-NFS-03 — closed: metadata acquisition and local owner display

Relevant current source: src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 75, 273–279 and 392.

NFS08/default and display-map-failed now request owner and owner_group with GETATTR after obtaining the verified filehandle. The returned object is explicitly metadata. The response matches the GETATTR request's XID, GSS sequence and NFS slot sequence. The client obtains the plaintext metadata only after protected response verification, accepts it, and then performs a separate client-local display conversion. The server identity-map action no longer writes a client display string.

The display-map-failed trace has GETATTR request at zero-based event 62, response 67, response verification 68, metadata acceptance 69 and client display conversion 70. Its separate server identity mapping occurs at 78, file dispatch at 83 and verified read result at 88. The new GETATTR advances the modeled session sequence: metadata uses slot sequence 2, READ uses 3 and CLOSE uses 4.

Both comparisons retain the same authenticated principal, server UID/GID/groups, mapping/export/file decisions, one READ dispatch and identical accepted file bytes. Display failure changes only the display outcome. Six distinct authorization denials—unmapped principal, file ACL, read-only export, unauthorized group, root squash and all squash—still produce neither the new display conversion nor file bytes. Returned owner metadata is not used as a credential or grant.

This satisfies the exact original NFS08 metadata/display requirement and preserves the distinction described by RFC 8881, §§5.9 and 18.7. It does not claim to implement every client name-service configuration or the full NFSv4 ACL model.

WIN-P6-01 — Request and result ownership

Q is created before validation with the original local SID, groups and privileges and a distinct NewCredentials LUID. Q receives an opaque context reference, sends its own SMB request and receives the result with the same request ID, operation and context reference. Every prefix excludes the original caller from result/data custody. Success file data appears at Q only after the accepted SMB READ and local handoff. Bad credentials, share denial, unavailable authority and connection reuse keep Q alive; the two early local denials return from the redirector to Q. The successful close releases Q’s context, opaque reference, token and process holdings.

WLOG08 was separately checked in all four variants: its original application remains the local network-result consumer, while local bob and outbound domain alice remain distinct. The no-Kerberos-prerequisite case still stops before the network helper.

WIN-P6-02 — Explicit TGS reply-key lineage

The helper creates a fresh request-bound authenticator subkey in the protected role and returns that independent subkey with the opaque authenticator. It never returns the protected TGT session key. The KDC obtains the subkey only after the TGT/authenticator/request verification step. The selected subkey protects the client reply and is used at client decryption; the machine account key independently protects the service ticket. The client acquires the host session key only after reply validation.

The authored checksum/authenticator/reply usages 6/7/9 agree with RFC 4120 §7.5.1. RFC 4120 §§3.3.1–3.3.4 permit the selected authenticator subkey to protect the TGS reply. This closes the missing key provenance; it does not claim that a native Windows trace demonstrated this precise internal IPC.

JK-01: request-specific refresh behavior

The correction in src/jwt-validation-lab.js:211–246 keeps originalTokenDecision separate from each flood arrival. A new independent probe checks all six JWT06 variants and their accepted-claims holdings at every complete event prefix; expected results are explicit reviewer assertions, not values imported from a worksheet.

In stale-cache, the original request fetches once, receives the configured issuer response, installs fresh keys, verifies the signature, checks claims and finally accepts them. The independent old-key request remains unaccepted while its cache is stale. The previous variant-name-driven failure is absent.

The flood case records all 32 separate request identities. The original generation2 request occupies one of the 16 pending slots. unknown0 through unknown14 coalesce; flood-token15 through flood-token31 receive 17 individual refresh-bounded errors with matching request IDs and kid values. All those rejection snapshots retain the original generation2 slot. There is exactly one refresh request. Completion clears pending state and records 15 missing unknown keys in the bounded negative cache; it does not put generation2 into that negative cache. The original request then succeeds. No flood token acquires accepted claims or resource permission.

The timeout, rate-budget and missing-new-key comparisons remain distinct and fail before accepted claims. Refresh policy constants remain an explicitly selected demo policy, rather than universal RFC or Kubernetes requirements.

JWT06 case Response Cache install Signature Claims Acceptance / denial
default 11 12 15 16 accept 17
stale-cache 11 12 15 16 accept 17
unknown-kid-flood 30 31 34 35 accept 36
refresh-timeout absent absent absent absent refresh-timeout at 10
retry-budget absent absent absent absent refresh-rate at 8; no fetch
missing-new-key 11 12 absent absent unknown-kid at selection 14

All coordinates are zero-based complete-event indices, including authored prepare events. The refresh request is index 6 in every case except retry-budget. Acceptance holdings remain absent before the acceptance event; resource authorization remains false throughout this validation lesson.

JK-02: actual selected key and plaintext boundary

The correction in src/jwt-validation-lab.js:146–162 constructs a concrete selected key object with stable ID, handle, algorithm and use. The private-key artifact supplies the validator input. The displayed result also identifies that artifact and the unchanged encryption public key, so the denial can be explained from visible custody rather than an invisible variant switch.

All four JWT03 cases were independently checked at every complete event prefix. At unwrap index 3, default obtains the CEK and readable inner token only after authenticated unwrap; contextual validation remains later. Wrong-recipient ends with recipient-key and changed-tag with aead-evidence, with neither plaintext nor CEK acquired by the API at any prefix. Invalid-inner-signature successfully unwraps and then fails the distinct inner signature step. The carrier never acquires CEK or inner plaintext, and the recipient private key remains recipient-local.

These corrections respect the key-selection and authenticated-decryption boundaries in RFC 7516 §5.2 and the separate outer/inner validation requirement in RFC 8725 §3.3. The runtime verdict remains explicitly symbolic; no numerical RSA-OAEP or full nested-JWE proof is inferred.

src/jwt-policy.js, src/held-object-jwt.js and tools/verification/expansion-crypto/next-jwt-vectors.mjs are also byte-identical. P6C-MCP-01 — P2: Add the required current-version result type to proxy tool-error responses

Location: source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:660.

Affected cases: MCP09 / upstream-expired and upstream-wrong-audience.

Exact observation: Both cases reach lab-mcp09:proxy-upstream-error-recover at zero-based event index 49, displayed step 50. The proxy now correctly returns HTTP 200 and a JSON-RPC tool execution error with isError:true, preserving downstream token acceptance. Its Body.result contains only isError and content; it omits resultType.

Expected: This sender advertises MCP 2026-07-28, whose Base Overview requires result responses to contain resultType. A completed tool execution error uses resultType:"complete"; the dated Tools error example shows this field together with isError:true.

Impact and scope: The newly authored wire shape does not conform to its selected sender profile. The dated specification also requires clients to treat absent resultType as complete for compatibility with older servers, so this review does not claim that every receiver rejects the current packet. No downstream credential loss, unauthorized execution or secret leakage was found. The existing A1 actor/verdict correction remains accepted separately.

Worker change: Add resultType:'complete' inside the result object of this shared proxy error response. Preserve its HTTP 200 tool-error mapping, matching request ID, isError:true, upstream-only renewal explanation and the separately accepted downstream context. Update the corresponding exact-field/worksheet expectations and the focused correction regression.

  1. For both affected variants, the actual recovered JSON-RPC result contains resultType:'complete', isError:true, the matching downstream request ID and the current upstream recovery text.
  2. Downstream accepted remains true, upstream accepted remains false, protected output remains unavailable, and neither upstream nor downstream token bytes appear in the returned error body.
  3. Check the other authored JSON-RPC result bodies remain complete; the independent scan found 22 recovered Body.result values and exactly these two omissions. The success paths already include the field.
  4. A focused MCP regression and regenerated affected field/trace evidence are sufficient for this field addition; preserve the root's existing integrated verification requirements without another unrelated native/performance sweep.

Reviewed 22 October 2026. Candidate standalone SHA256: 1ee48718e7623bb69c7063591561a38a2d7170f87e9f7816f3d8aeead127a40e. Supplied-plan SHA256: 5a8478ea904e0862da5b0a6e978b7e7389399ffb62890d4e1c7bbee92774a4a0.

Findings

P6-NFS-01 — P1 — Every successful v4 OPEN invents a returned filehandle without GETFH

Location: source/src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 236, 237, 250, 252.

Actual: The authored COMPOUND ends at OPEN. The OPEN result nevertheless carries stateid and filehandle; open-accept installs that handle at the client. v4.0 subsequently uses the invented handle in OPEN_CONFIRM.

Expected: OPEN updates server CURRENT_FH and returns OPEN state, not an on-wire filehandle. GETFH must follow OPEN in the same COMPOUND; the client obtains its filehandle from that GETFH result.

Impact: A central visible operation list, response payload and custody transition teach an invalid v4 protocol exchange in 28 reachable cases across 10 core rows.

Reproduction: {"scenario": "lab-nfs-v42-kerberos-read", "case": "default", "requestStep": 47, "requestIndex": 46, "responseStep": 58, "responseIndex": 57, "acceptStep": 60, "acceptIndex": 59, "requestStage": "namespace-open", "responseStage": "open-response", "acceptStage": "open-accept", "operations": ["SEQUENCE", "PUTROOTFH", "LOOKUP", "OPEN"]}.

Worker fix:

  1. Append GETFH after OPEN to the actual namespace operations and displayed request for v4.0, v4.1 and v4.2, including the SECINFO retry.
  2. Attribute the stateid to OPEN and filehandle to GETFH in the COMPOUND result; preserve protected receipt and client-local verification.
  3. Retain correct v4.0 OPEN_CONFIRM and v4.1+ SEQUENCE handling; do not transplant GETFH into NFSv3 LOOKUP.

Independent verification:

  • Independently inspect every reachable successful OPEN operation list for a later GETFH in the same COMPOUND.
  • Assert filehandle provenance is the GETFH result and no client custody exists before protected receipt/verification.
  • Check NFS05 OPEN_CONFIRM consumes that verified GETFH handle; retain NFS07 post-SECINFO CURRENT_FH rules.

Authority: RFC8881 18.16.2,18.16.4.1,18.8; RFC7530 16.16.2,16.16.4. Evidence: nfs-independent-probe.json:openWithoutGetfh.

P6-NFS-02 — P2 — Post-Finished TLS denial alerts encrypt/decrypt without application traffic keys

Location: source/src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 99, 103, 107, 110, 445, 456, 458, 460, 461, 462.

Actual: Client identity and host-policy failures return before directional application-secret creation. deny(tlsAlert:true) still emits encrypt/decrypt operations, but selects neither server nor client key. The corrupt-application-record variant has secrets but also omits key use.

Expected: After the server has sent Finished, server alerts responding to the client Certificate/CertificateVerify use the server application traffic key. Each endpoint must possess and use its own locally derived directional copy; key derivation does not establish mTLS admission.

Impact: Negative flows have impossible cryptographic lineage and conceal the distinction between available application keys and an admitted authenticated transport.

Reproduction: {"scenario": "lab-nfs-required-tls-failure", "case": "missing-client-identity", "serverFinishedStep": 14, "createAlertStep": 23, "wireAlertStep": 24, "acceptAlertStep": 25, "applicationSecretArtifacts": []}.

Worker fix:

  1. Derive local application secrets from the correct HKDF/master-secret state and transcript through server Finished before an applicable post-Finished alert.
  2. Bind server alert encryption to tls-s2c-server and client decryption to tls-s2c-client, or equivalently explicit correct locally owned key artifacts.
  3. Keep transport acceptance false for failed mTLS/host policy and stop NFS dispatch; deriving keys must not mark authentication successful.
  4. Preserve local ownership and appropriate disposal on failed connection closure.

Independent verification:

  • Check all five pre-derivation denial cases have correct directional local key custody before alert creation/decryption.
  • Check corrupt-application-record uses the existing server/client S2C copies.
  • Assert no plaintext key transfer, no client file bytes, no successful admission or NFS dispatch in these denials.

Authority: RFC9846 4.5.3,5.2,7.1. Evidence: nfs-independent-probe.json:alertsWithoutApplicationKeys.

P6-NFS-03 — P2 — NFS08 omits the required metadata-read and separate owner-display mapping flow

Location: source/src/nfs-access-lab.js, lines 370.

Actual: The server-policy identity-map action writes a final ownerDisplay string. No GETATTR operation, owner/owner_group metadata artifact or client-local display mapping exists. The failure variant changes the string while READ remains allowed.

Expected: The lesson separately shows acquisition of owner/owner_group metadata and client-side display mapping, distinct from authenticated-principal-to-server-local-identity authorization mapping.

Impact: A required teaching flow is represented only by a server-side final-state assertion, leaving the requested distinction and held-object custody unobservable.

Reproduction: {"scenario": "lab-nfs-identity-permission", "cases": ["default", "display-map-failed"], "stateWriterStep": 68, "stateWriterIndex": 67, "stateWriterStage": "identity-map", "stateWriterActor": "nfsPolicy", "metadataOperations": [], "metadataArtifacts": []}.

Worker fix:

  1. Add a bounded metadata acquisition using GETATTR with owner/owner_group, protected response receipt/acceptance and a separate client display-mapping action.
  2. Represent the returned owner/owner_group strings as metadata rather than authenticated caller credentials or an authorization grant.
  3. Make display-map-failed fail only the local display conversion; keep server principal mapping/export/file policy independent and allow the same authorized READ.

Independent verification:

  • Default and display-map-failed must expose metadata request/result, client receipt before local conversion and correct held-object prefixes.
  • Assert display mapping failure leaves the authenticated principal, server effective UID/groups and authorized READ unchanged.
  • Retain actual server mapping-denied and file-denied cases as separate outcomes.

Authority: Exact supplied plan NFS08 step3; source/docs/next-expansion/nfs-worksheet.json NFS08.requiredFlow[2]; RFC8881 5.9,18.7. Evidence: nfs-independent-probe.json:displayMapping.

Coverage against all 13 core rows

Row Authored cases Review

Custody, authorization and replay observations

  • RPCSEC_GSS authentication, integrity and privacy have distinct body-protection semantics. Readable integrity-protected data remains untrusted until receiver verification; privacy keeps the wire form separate. AUTH_SYS is an asserted UID/GID and remains so under a host-authenticated TLS connection.
  • User and machine contexts are separate. The client TGT is not sent to the NFS server, and the client does not receive the NFS service long-term key. Machine session-state permission does not itself grant Alice file access.
  • Export, mapping, squash and file-permission checks are separate from protocol authentication. The bounded POSIX-mode fixture is disclosed as such; it is not presented as the complete NFSv4 ACE algorithm.
  • RPCSEC_GSS duplicate/below-window handling is distinct from NFS session replay. The latter reuses the NFS slot request with a fresh acceptable GSS sequence and cached NFS result without duplicate file dispatch.
  • SECINFO query responses are tuple discovery, not a grant. The legal LOOKUP boundary and consumed CURRENT_FH are modeled. The successful retry still needs the GETFH correction described above.
  • The held-object adapter projects the authored ledger consistently; that consistency does not validate the ledger against a protocol. The three findings identify ledger-level deficiencies that shared final-state tests do not expose.
  • The NFS09 AS cross-link was explicitly checked in the constructed model: lab-ad-cache-tgt is appended at source line542. There is no missing-link finding.

Independent probe and evidence

Run node nfs-independent-probe.mjs from this directory. This read-only probe imports the shipped models, constructs all 83 authored cases and checks specific counterexamples. Current results: 28 OPEN/GETFH counterexamples, 6 TLS alert-key counterexamples, and 2 NFS08 metadata/display counterexamples. It writes nfs-independent-probe.json. It intentionally detects present defects rather than declaring conformance when implementation-generated states agree.

The detailed JSON report records case/step identifiers and verification requirements. Displayed step ordinals are one-based; corresponding index values are zero-based. These are symbolic traces: no native mount, kernel build, packet capture, TLS crypto implementation or Linux/Windows interoperability run was performed. The product accurately bounds those claims; this review does not broaden them.

Primary sources checked

  • RFC8881, §§5.9, 18.7, 18.8, 18.16.2, 18.16.4.1, 18.29, 18.45: NFSv4.1 operations, owner metadata, OPEN/GETFH, security discovery.
  • RFC7530, §§16.16.2, 16.16.4: NFSv4.0 OPEN result and mandatory following GETFH.
  • RFC9846, §§4.5.3, 5.2, 7.1: Current TLS1.3 Finished/application traffic protection and key schedule.
  • RFC2203, §§5.3.3.1, 5.3.3.4.2, 5.3.3.4.3: RPCSEC_GSS sequence replay and body-verification error behavior.
  • RFC9289, §§4.1: AUTH_TLS support discovery and same-connection upgrade.

Use the current TLS1.3 RFC9846 wording for the alert finding: its Finished section explicitly covers server alerts sent in response to the client certificate/proof after server Finished. RFC8881 and RFC7530 both explicitly require GETFH after OPEN in the same COMPOUND; this is a normative operation/result defect rather than a request for extra UI verbosity.

WIN-P6-01 — P2: Return /netonly network results to the launched process Q

Actual: The fixture creates separate parent and child actors/tokens and a NewCredentials context. The shared SMB helper nevertheless hardcodes result readers, success-data plaintext readers, and network-handoff destination to wslProcess. No wslChild-to-wslNetwork request exists in any of the five cases. Merely placing the NewCredentials context ID in the result does not establish the requesting-process/custody boundary.

Sources and limits

  • S1: CreateProcessWithLogonW — dwLogonFlags / LOGON_NETCREDENTIALS_ONLY. The new process retains caller local identity but receives a new LSA logon session with specified outbound credentials; credentials are not validated at launch.

  • S2: RFC 4120 — 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 3.3.3 and 5.4.2. The TGS reply encrypted part uses the authenticator sub-session key when supplied, otherwise the TGT session key. This is distinct from the service key protecting the service ticket.

  • S3: How Credential Guard works — LSA/LSAIso architecture and Credential Guard protection limits. LSA communicates with isolated LSA through RPC. TGT protection differs from service-ticket protection; cached verifiers are local validation material, not remote credentials.

  • P1: Supplied worker plan embedded scenario ledger (review/inputs/worker-plan.html) — WELEV05 steps network/result; WLOG02 acceptance; WELEV03 cleanup; windowsSharedContracts.modelRules. The plan explicitly distinguishes original P from new Q, requires network result at Q, source/protection/acceptance events, and a correlated launch outcome.

  • This is a targeted source, exact-plan and deterministic held-object/state review. Enumeration of 86 cases is coverage evidence, not blanket semantic acceptance or installed-Windows interoperability.

  • Native token/ETW/Windows build observations were not performed. WLOG05 modern algorithm/freshness gates, offline smart-card/WHfB research boundaries and WELEV06 support/CSP-label discrepancy remain disclosed reference limitations, not newly invented blockers.

  • Accepted WIN11 and broader baseline preservation are owned by the root review; this review makes no independent fresh acceptance claim for the entire legacy corpus.

  • The existing five material performance regressions, 22 variable comparison cells, manual G01 screen-reader acceptance and other disclosed historical/cross-engine limits are not reclassified as Windows semantic findings. The four optional extensions remain deferred.

Reproduce from the P6 directory: node independent-validation/windows-review-probe.mjs. This writes reviewer evidence only. Product-file SHA-256 values are recorded in windows-review.json.

P6 independent Linux/macOS review

Changes requested: three causal/admission/policy defects, one core lifecycle coverage gap, and two lower-priority state/presentation inconsistencies.

Reviewed all 17 core rows / 156 canonical cases against the embedded worker plan. Source inspection and independent model/custody probes; no product changes, full-suite rerun or native-platform claim.

Findings

UNIX-01 — P2: PAM new-password policy is decided before the new password exists

Category: causal authentication flow. Location: source/src/linux-logon-lab.js:347; source/src/linux-logon-lab.js:348.

Exact reproduction: Select LLOG04 / new-policy-denied; inspect cursor 7 and the complete event/object list. unix-probe.json passwordPolicyBeforeInput.secretCreated is false. Default also has password-preliminary before new-secret.

Actual: new-policy-denied sets newPasswordPolicyAccepted=false and emits password-policy-deny without ever creating or collecting new-secret. The success branch also decides new-password policy in password-preliminary before new-secret collection.

Expected: Keep preliminary old-credential/readiness checks separate. Collect the proposed new token, then evaluate its configured policy before committing an authority update. Plan LLOG04 explicitly requires that order.

Impact: The teaching flow invents a password-policy rejection without its required input. This is an incorrect causal explanation, not a successful unauthorized login.

Worker action: Move new-password policy evaluation after new-secret collection, distinguish preliminary from update phases, and consume the new-token object at the decision. Clean old/new transient secrets on rejection and retain authority generation 1.

Verification: Assert both positive and policy-denied traces collect the candidate before evaluating it; denial has no authority commit or session, while cleanup removes the candidate from both holders. Do not merely assert a precomputed policy flag.

Sources: Upstream Linux-PAM manual reproduced by man7; Official Linux-PAM source; current master independently inspected, not independently reverified worker commit.

UNIX-02 — P2: Platform SSO exemption itself authenticates the local user

Category: false admission in model. Location: source/src/macos-logon-lab.js:124.

Exact reproduction: Select MLOG05 / exempt-account; cursor 2 is the exemption event and no local-password event exists. Run createMacPlatformSSOCase({...exemptFixture,localPassword:false}); see unix-probe.json exemptAccount.constructorProbe. This wrong-password combination is a constructor probe, not an existing selectable case.

Actual: The selectable exempt-account trace changes authenticated to true at local-exemption and creates a local session without a local-password decision. The exported constructor with that same fixture plus localPassword=false also ends authenticated/admitted/session=true.

Expected: An exempt local account skips Platform SSO registration and its login policies, but still passes ordinary local authentication and admission. Exemption is not an authentication factor.

Impact: A configured Platform SSO exemption is taught as sufficient to open a desktop, and the local-password predicate is ignored on this branch.

Worker action: Route the exempt branch through an explicit local password/selected local-method gate before open(). Preserve idpSSO=false. Add a selectable failed-local-proof exempt-account case or an equivalent explicit negative predicate.

Verification: Correct local password can admit an eligible exempt local account without IdP registration; failed local proof yields no session or IdP SSO. Replay must not briefly show authenticated=true at the exemption decision.

Sources: Apple Platform Deployment; Set up Platform SSO and Login policies.

Full core-row disposition

“No new finding” means no issue found within this symbolic/documentation review; it is not native platform certification.

JK-01 — P2 — Keep JWT06 refresh results attached to the request that caused them; do not force stale-cache rejection

Location: src/jwt-validation-lab.js lines 205–215; src/jwt-policy.js:84-96.

Cases: stale-cache, unknown-kid-flood.

Replay: lab-jwt06:refresh-deny (stale-cache), zero-based cursor 10:1; lab-jwt06:refresh-deny (unknown-kid-flood), zero-based cursor 12:1.

Actual: stale-cache obtains action=refresh, sends a refresh request, then the variant-name disjunct forces failure with code stale-cache and an error artifact whose action remains refresh. unknown-kid-flood overwrites the generation2 request decision with flood-token15 / unknown15 capacity rejection, then attaches that rejection to the original generation2 token and stops its pending refresh.

Expected: A stale cache does not authenticate a token from old material, but it can refresh when budget permits. The original generation2 token has a reserved pending slot. A new excess request may be rejected without cancelling or reclassifying that original request. With the supplied keys and a response at now+1, both original requests validate successfully under the declared policy.

Why this matters: The lesson teaches a false stale-cache failure and conflates the identity of independent requests. This defeats the explicit request-specific bounded-coalescing and detector provenance contract even though these branches reach the worksheet expected terminal failures.

Reproduce: From source/: node ../independent-validation/jwt-k8s-probe.mjs. Inspect refresh entries and their matching model failure artifacts. The independently driven helper returns originalRecheck=coalesced/refresh-in-flight and originalValidationAfterTimelyRefresh.ok=true in both cases.

Worker change: Remove variant-name-driven terminal branching. Keep originalTokenDecision separate from each flood request decision. Emit capacity errors with the actual rejected request instance/kid; finish the one in-flight refresh for admitted requests. If stale-cache is intended as a denial lesson, author a concrete failed/late refresh or unavailable response, and name that actual detector instead of treating staleness itself as a terminal failure.

Acceptance:

  • With a stale initial cache and timely successful JWKS response, no stale material is accepted, refresh succeeds, and only then the new token claims are accepted.
  • With 32 unknown-kid arrivals, pending/negative storage stays bounded and one fetch occurs; overflow rejection identifies unknown15/flood-token15 (or the correct first excess request).
  • The original generation2 request remains pending and can succeed after the timely response; unrelated old-token freshness behavior remains independent.
  • Refresh rejection artifacts always carry action=deny and the exact denied request identity. Update source-first expectations and replay targets rather than preserving an incorrect worksheet oracle.

This is a violation of the authored demo policy and exact artifact contract, not an assertion that any RFC mandates the 300s/30s/2s/16-entry choices.

Sources: review/inputs/worker-plan.html — worker-scenario-ledger JWT06 steps2-3 and negativeCases; docs/next-expansion/jwt-policy-contract.md — Refresh pending tracking / public cache helper API.

JK-02 — P2 — Make the wrong-recipient JWE case actually hold and use the wrong recipient key

Location: src/jwt-validation-lab.js lines 141–154; src/jwt-policy.js:76-81.

Cases: wrong-recipient.

Replay: lab-jwt03:unwrap (wrong-recipient), zero-based cursor 3:1.

Actual: The validator receives recipientKeyId=recipient-other and rejects recipient-key. The key artifact used in the unwrap event is still HANDLE(recipient-RSA-OAEP-256-private-generation1), identical to the successful default. The outer recipient public key and decryption evidence both name recipient-generation1.

Expected: The selected private-key artifact, its identity/handle and the validator recipientKeyId must agree. If this is a wrong-key lesson, the selected/held private key must visibly be recipient-other, distinct from the recipient-generation1 public key that encrypted the CEK.

Why this matters: The visible custody state shows the correct recipient key while the decision depends on a different invisible key input. Learners cannot explain the failure from the held evidence; this is precisely the key-selection boundary the scenario is supposed to teach.

Reproduce: Run the same independent probe. Compare jwe default versus wrong-recipient privateKeyArtifact.value, encryptionPublicKey.id, validatorRecipientKeyId and decrypt-evidence. The private key value does not change; the hidden validation selector does.

Worker change: Create/select a distinct recipient-other private-key artifact for this variant, attach a stable key ID to its representation, and pass that ID to jwtDecryptFixture from the selected artifact. Preserve the original public recipient key/envelope. Bind decrypt evidence and held operations to those actual artifact identities.

Acceptance:

  • At initial and unwrap cursors, wrong-recipient visibly holds/uses recipient-other rather than generation1; default continues to use generation1.
  • The unwrap verdict recipientKeyId equals the selected key artifact identity.
  • Wrong-recipient and changed-tag acquire neither CEK nor inner plaintext; default authenticated unwrap does, and invalid inner signature still fails later.
  • Inspect source-held inventory and emitted held presentation at cursor3:1; a final failure-state assertion alone is insufficient.

Runtime decryption is explicitly symbolic; the finding concerns faithful representation of recipient-key selection, not a claim of a vulnerable production JWE implementation.

Sources: review/inputs/worker-plan.html — worker-scenario-ledger JWT03 preconditions, held state, negativeCases; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7516.html#section-5.2 — 5.2 steps7,9,15-16; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725.html#section-3.3 — 3.3.

P6-MCP-01 — P2: Step-up changes the original operation and confuses requested versus granted scopes

Disposition: required correction.

Where: source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:492; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:493; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:573; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:449; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:454; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:456; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:473; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:572.

Scenarios/cases: MCP06; default, challenge-outside-metadata, smaller-grant, hierarchy-not-permission, upgrade-acl-denied.

Exact replay checkpoints:

  • lab-mcp06:write-request-recover — zero-based event 2, journey step 3, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:operation-host-approval — zero-based event 42, journey step 43, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:operation-construct — zero-based event 43, journey step 44, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:operation-policy — zero-based event 50, journey step 51, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:operation-result-accept — zero-based event 55, journey step 56, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:stepup-check — zero-based event 9, journey step 10, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:stepup-grant-authorization-recover — zero-based event 15, journey step 16, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:stepup-grant-token-response-recover — zero-based event 38, journey step 39, completed milestone.
  • lab-mcp06:operation-policy — zero-based event 50, journey step 51, completed milestone.

Expected: Carry the same write operation, target and arguments through consent and retry. The host approval, Mcp-Name header, JSON-RPC params.name and resource scope check must all describe that operation. A successful read is not evidence that the original write completed. Related smaller-grant defect: Request the computed union files:read files:write, then separately model the AS granting fewer/different scopes. Preserve both exact sets; where the issued access scope differs from that request, return the granted scope in the token response.

Actual: The original POST uses write_file (index 2). After step-up, the host approves read_file (42), the retry header/body use read_file (43), but resource policy requires files:write (50); the sequence then reports operationExecuted/resultLearned=true. mcpInvoke hardcodes read_file and receives only a scope override from MCP06. Related smaller-grant defect: stepup-check computes read+write at index 9. The smaller-grant branch passes only files:read as mcpGrant.scopes, so the actual authorization request at index 15 asks only for read. The returned token has exactly the request scope and the token response contains only token_type/expires_in. Thus the authored sequence never demonstrates an AS reducing a read+write request, despite its branch label and plan contract. hierarchy-not-permission similarly sends the selected grant as the request.

Why it matters: The core read-to-write lesson grants a success conclusion to a different operation and teaches an inconsistent tool-to-permission mapping. Negative variants can also reject a read solely for lacking write scope. Related smaller-grant defect: The displayed union and actual OAuth request disagree. The required requested-versus-granted lesson is absent and its apparent negative coverage is misleading.

Basis: MCP step-up instructions retry the original request. The exact plan MCP06 steps 3–5 require preserving requested/granted sets and reevaluating the write policy. Related smaller-grant defect: The plan explicitly separates requested and granted sets. MCP requires the computed step-up set to be used for reauthorization. OAuth 2.1 -13 sections 1.4.1/3.2.3 define actual-scope reporting when grant and request differ.

Sources: MCP Authorization, dated 2026-07-28; OAuth 2.1, draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-13.

Reproduce: Run node mcp-review-probe.mjs; inspect observations.stepupChangedOperation. In the product select MCP06/default and compare steps 3, 43, 44 and 51. Related smaller-grant defect: Run node mcp-review-probe.mjs; compare observations.stepupSmallerGrant.decision.fields.Decision.requested with authorization.fields.scope and the token response.

Worker change: Give mcpInvoke an explicit immutable operation descriptor (tool, target, arguments and required scopes), pass write_file from MCP06 and use it consistently in host approval, mirrored HTTP/JSON metadata, policy and result. Retain the original descriptor for the bounded retry. Related smaller-grant defect: Separate requestedScopes and grantedScopes in the grant builder; use requestedScopes in the authorization request and grantedScopes in consent/token issuance. Include scope in the token response when required and let the client learn the actual grant from that response before retrying.

Acceptance check: Assert that initial and retried name/arguments are identical, that approval references the write operation, and that the write result is emitted only after write scope and ACL acceptance. Recheck default, smaller-grant and upgrade-acl-denied at exact prefixes, not just the final boolean. Related smaller-grant defect: For smaller-grant, independently expect request scope read+write, response/token scope read only, no write execution and preservation of the prior read grant. Confirm the negative differs from default in the AS grant rather than silently in the client request.

For invalid tokens include the appropriate invalid_token parameter; for absent credentials avoid pretending a token failed validation. Include the profile metadata pointer and required scope where applicable. Correct canonical packet expectations rather than merely adding descriptive prose.

Check scope-error header values against the challenged operation. Keep token-endpoint errors in their own error domain.

P6-MCP-03 — P2: Refresh scope escalation is mislabeled invalid_grant and disposes a valid refresh token

Disposition: required correction.

Where: source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:319; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:322; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:579; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:583; source/src/mcp-auth-lab.js:584.

  • lab-mcp07:reauthorize-required — zero-based event 9, journey step 10, completed milestone.

Expected: Distinguish a valid refresh credential with an excessive requested scope from an invalid/revoked/reused grant. Return invalid_scope for the former and preserve the valid grant; broader permission requires new consent, while a refresh with the original permitted scope remains a distinct option.

Actual: The exact refresh-check input at index 4 says valid=true, revoked=false, generation=currentGeneration=1, correct client/resource, allowed files:read; only the request asks files:admin. The combined condition returns invalid_grant with reauthorize=true. The response repeats invalid_grant at index 8; cleanup at index 9 removes the client refresh-g1 holding even though no refresh invalidation occurred at A. The AS retains its refresh holding.

Why it matters: The lesson teaches that a scope-request mistake invalidates the underlying refresh grant, conflating request rejection with credential invalidity and forcing unnecessary reauthorization.

Basis: OAuth 2.1 -13 section 3.2.4 distinguishes invalid_scope (including scope exceeding the grant) from invalid_grant. The plan only instructs disposal of unusable credentials; this fixture explicitly begins with a valid one.

Sources: OAuth 2.1, draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-13.

Reproduce: Run node mcp-review-probe.mjs; observations.refreshScopeError includes request, authority verdict, response, cleanup and initial/final exact refresh holdings.

Worker change: Evaluate grant validity separately from requested scope. Represent invalid_scope as an actual AS token-endpoint response and retain the existing valid refresh generation. Explain how new consent can obtain broader scope; reserve invalid_grant and associated disposal for genuinely invalid, revoked, expired or reused credentials. Review resource escalation against RFC 8707 independently rather than folding every constraint into invalid_grant.

Acceptance check: Keep one valid-grant/excess-scope case expecting invalid_scope and retained refresh; keep a separate rotated/revoked case expecting invalid_grant. Assert no new access generation and no resource invocation on the rejected request. Prove the original permitted-scope refresh can still be considered without claiming the failed request revoked its grant.

Actual: MCP03 A fetches the client URL at index 9 before any C/B-to-A authorization message or initial A holding supplies it. A validates at 13 and sends a separate registration-verdict to C at 16. C only then creates the OAuth transaction and browser authorization at 21; B reaches A at 24. There is no authored prior AS cache/registration/request that explains the early URL/redirect knowledge, and CIMD does not define this standalone A-to-C registration acknowledgment.

Why it matters: The advertised current CIMD lesson is rendered as a DCR-like preflight handshake with unexplained AS knowledge, obscuring the main mechanism: on-demand resolution of the URL client_id in an authorization transaction.

Basis: CIMD draft -00 sections 4, 4.3 and 6.4 tie client metadata lookup to the authorization request; MCP registration requires resolution/validation of URL identifiers and the request redirect. The original plan MCP03 unfortunately lists obtaining/recording metadata before resuming a fresh authorization transaction. This is a correction to that reviewer sequencing, not a claim that the worker ignored an unambiguous plan.

Sources: OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents, draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-00; MCP Client Registration, dated 2026-07-28.

Reproduce: Run node mcp-review-probe.mjs; observations.cimdOrder records every relevant event and A holdings before the fetch. Inspect the default timeline in that order.

Worker change: Clarify MCP03 plan sequencing and split the grant builder at request receipt: create transaction, carry complete authorization parameters to A, fetch/validate CIMD at A, then authenticate/consent and issue code in that transaction. Keep the validated registration/configuration as A-local evidence; remove the invented network registration-verdict unless an explicitly sourced alternative protocol is selected. Failure must be tied to the received request and correctly scoped error path.

Acceptance check: Assert A cannot fetch this URL before receiving it in the authorization request (unless an explicit preexisting cache is intentionally modeled). Validate exact client_id and redirect at the A checkpoint; prove failures stop code/token issuance. Confirm the pre-registered and deprecated DCR variants remain behaviorally distinct.

Advisory

P6-MCP-A1 — P3: Expose two proxy authorization verdicts instead of one changing Resource token accepted badge

MCP09 upstream-expired preserves downstreamTokenAccepted=true and its accepted downstream context holding. However, mcpValidateToken writes the shared tokenAccepted=false for U, and the common decision binding displays only Resource token accepted. It does not expose separate downstream/upstream verdict bindings. The proxy then sends C an HTTP:401 field after U rejected the independent upstream token.

Add explicit Downstream C→P token accepted and Upstream P→U token accepted bindings. Show which issuer/resource owns renewal and keep the downstream grant visibly accepted. Author the P→C failure as a deliberate mapping of the upstream API failure rather than implying C must replace its valid P token. MCP Tools describes API failures as tool execution errors, but this review does not mandate a universal HTTP 502 or a single error encoding for every deployment.

Acceptance: At upstream rejection, show downstream=true/upstream=false side by side, retain the downstream context, leak neither credential, and have the recovery action address the upstream grant.

No full-suite or performance rerun, browser/native interoperability check or G01 manual acceptance was performed by this subreview. The consolidated review above records those gates.

Explicit non-findings

P6 UX review

One confirmed P2 usability defect, inherited from the baseline, should be corrected before usability acceptance. The six fresh mounted navigation/content checks pass. Current performance and manual G01 remain open.

P6-UX-01 — Primary Play/Resume loses contrast on hover

source/src/styles.css:158–160 supplies a generic .button:hover:not(:disabled) background with higher specificity than .button.primary. The primary hover rule changes only the brightness filter, so the generic dark hover background remains paired with dark primary text. This is shared CSS and already exists in the accepted WIN-11 source; it is a newly identified issue, not a new expansion regression or a reopening of a previously fixed finding.

Reproduce in any full journey with an enabled Play/Pause/Resume button: hover it in dark mode. Supplied WLOG01 step2/15, AD child-domain step1/31 and SSH certificate step24/35 captures visibly show the near-invisible Resume label. Read-only pixel samples give solid background RGB(31,47,73) and text RGB(40,31,91), contrast about 1.086:1. Normal BasicKeycloak capture retains its purple background. The source colors before brightness are1.079:1; the light theme predicts white on #eaf0fa, also inadequate.

The normal label is12px. W3C SC1.4.3 guidance requires4.5:1 for ordinary text and applies to hover/focus text. These enabled controls do not qualify for the inactive-control exception. The dark result is visible in actual supplied screenshots; light-theme output is a stylesheet inference, not a fresh native observation.

Worker fix: explicitly set a suitable primary hover background/foreground in the primary hover rule, or exclude primary buttons from generic hover. Preserve focus outlines and disabled behavior. Verify enabled Play/Pause/Resume and replay controls in both themes, default/hover/focus and any sticky touch-hover state. Use a focused native check; no full protocol sweep is needed for this CSS correction.

No product code changed.

assert.equal(out.positiveControls.ssrf.endState.credentialRequests,0);

Worker implementation plan · 21 October 2026

Auth Flow Studio — next expansion

Stabilization, NFS, workstation logon and elevation, JWT, Kubernetes access, and MCP authorization. One complete handoff, built on the independently accepted SMB correction snapshot.

Implement in reviewable phases. Start with the small WIN-11 repair and performance characterization, then NFS. Continue through workstation/elevation, JWT, Kubernetes and MCP. The core scenario ledger is committed scope; named negative inputs are required tests, while explicitly optional extensions remain separate.

1. Worker instructions

This file is the authoritative next implementation plan. Use the accepted source named below. The previous expansion plan and reviews remain history and preservation requirements; this plan replaces their queued-feature notes with concrete scope. Do not reopen the twenty-three closed findings or reinterpret pending features as already implemented.

  1. Verify the baseline hashes and inspect repository instructions before editing. If your working tree already contains later changes, compare them explicitly; do not overwrite them to recreate this snapshot.
  2. Create the new scenario/source/acceptance manifests before building the models. Use the plan IDs to track coverage; keep existing public scenario IDs and routes stable. Implement one complete representative per family before multiplying variants.
  3. For each phase, deliver working model events, canonical object holdings, field and exact-object replay, profile/source guidance, useful negative outcomes, navigation and the tests specified here. A label or explanatory paragraph does not substitute for an authored flow.
  4. Pin the operating-system/product build and protocol profile. Resolve the specifically flagged source conflicts before claiming platform support. Continue independent work while a narrow research item is unresolved; retain it visibly in the disposition instead of silently dropping it.
  5. Supply a standalone HTML, buildable source and matching verification evidence at each review boundary. Record which phase and exact bytes are being submitted. Finish the core ledger in phases; phase ordering is not permission to omit later core rows.

This task is an offline educational product expansion. All credentials, keys, certificates, identities, addresses and payloads are synthetic. The application must not contact live directories, clusters, identity providers or metadata endpoints. Publication follows the project’s existing process; this planning file performs no deployment or external communication.

Known baseline verification1,505 passing tests in 87 files; 214 compiled choices; byte-identical rebuild. These are historical baseline results, not results for future changes.

Preserve all 214 existing choices and their routes: web/OIDC/SAML/passkeys; SSH; standalone AD DS Kerberos, PKINIT, FAST and multi-forest trusts; Kerberos-to-Keycloak; NTLM/Negotiate/CredSSP/RDP/WinRM; RADIUS/EAP; SPAKE/PAKE; and all twelve SMB 3.1.1 scenarios. Preserve the supplied favicon assets; logo design remains deferred.

The original nineteen findings plus NET-05, WIN-09, WIN-10 and SMB-R01 are closed. WIN-11 is the single minor follow-up below. Manual G01 and current-build comparative performance remain open. Keep existing negative fixtures, exact-value propagation, receipt/acceptance boundaries and reader restrictions throughout the expansion.

Reuse versus new coverage: workstation orchestration may reuse the accepted Kerberos exchanges, but must add actual logon/session/token transitions. NFS requires its own RPC/security/file-authorization model; it is not a relabeled SMB flow. Kubernetes and MCP may reuse OAuth/JWT primitives, but require their distinct relying-party, token-purpose and authorization behavior.

5. Initial cleanup and performance work

P0-A — WIN-11, retain the already-correct key model

In src/windows-auth-lab.js, the raw CredSSP AP-REP path creates the acceptor subkey in held-object effects but omits that creation from field-only replay. The local-object selection around lines 181–191 and raw AP-REP construction around line 397 are the reviewed locations; verify them against your checkout.

Six fixed presets W09/W11/W13/W14/W15/W16 and seven named variants are affected: W09 binding-direction/binding-nonce/binding-public-key; W14 and W15 hybrid-without-early-result; W16 redirect-disconnect/hybrid-without-early-result. Author H’s real local create operation with the same artifact, value and source index. Preserve the H-owned held creation, then C’s acquisition only at mutual verification. Never add the secret key to the transmitted object list to make replay discover it.

Acceptance: all thirteen affected field paths begin with H creation, existing exact-object history remains correct, C has no plain key at wire receipt, and early initiator-key versus completed acceptor-key selection stays intact. One focused regression covering the shared builder paths is sufficient for this isolated fix.

P0-B — measure first; keep historical and current comparisons separate

Capture the accepted current artifact before feature work. Compare the optimized artifact against those exact bytes using the same environment, browser, viewport, loading mode, journey and input. Cover startup, existing-journey selection, idle search, replay start and search during playback. Measure the global field index open and closed, preserving normal default behavior; hiding the index is not by itself a completed usability fix.

Use source HTTP, standalone HTTP and standalone file, with fresh isolated browser contexts and at least the existing three samples per comparison. Retain raw samples and medians; add samples if variation prevents a useful conclusion. Preserve the existing material-change rule: both >25% and >50 ms for interactions, or both >25% and >100 ms for startup. These are project review thresholds, not statistical significance claims.

Profile separately from uninstrumented timing. Optimize the measured bottleneck—such as repeated index work, rendering or eager scenario setup—while preserving search completeness, exact selection, keyboard focus, reset/replay semantics and canonical object state. Recheck the same comparison after each substantive optimization; record unresolved results rather than changing thresholds to manufacture a pass.

The seven historical flags were measured on 92ab17825e1a410940edc7b52a4a1a2f8f7e252c3dd340499a7ce420e3775775 against the older accepted baseline. A new before/after comparison against 9a3fc759… measures this expansion’s incremental effect; it does not automatically clear that older regression. Reproduce the historical comparison with its exact baseline if claiming closure. If unavailable, keep its status explicit.

P0-C — manual G01 and navigation

Keep manual assistive-technology speech/comprehension acceptance as an explicit release gate, with an owner, chosen browser/AT combination, steps, observed output and unresolved problems. Do not claim it from simulated DOM focus or screenshots. Continue implementation and automatic verification while that gate remains open; never relabel “not performed” as passed.

Design scalable grouped navigation before adding the catalog. Preserve existing routes and favorites/deep links. Put JWT in Foundations, add dedicated Workstations, Files, Kubernetes and MCP groups, and make Files link to the existing canonical SMB family. Avoid duplicate SMB registrations and an overcrowded row of small tabs. Detailed keyboard, focus and responsive acceptance is in the integration section.

Each core row is a required fixed picker choice. Its named negative inputs and comparisons are required branch coverage, not extra registered choices. The four optional extensions are NFS14, WELEV07, K8S16 and MCP14. A protocol feature or deployment topology may be optional in the real world while its comparison lesson is required here; this is why MCP09–MCP10 remain core.

Research gates qualify implementation and support claims; they do not silently remove a core row. If a gate remains unresolved, mark that row partial and identify the exact missing evidence. Runtime IDs in the embedded ledger are proposed mappings: freeze the mapping before code, retain it across title changes, and never reuse an existing ID for different semantics. NFS access: implementation plan

Research cut: 21 October2026. Baseline: the accepted corrections2 source; preserve all214 choices and all12 SMB scenarios. This adds a discoverable NFS family and does not reopen accepted Network/RADIUS fixes.

Build NFS01–NFS13. NFS01 is the modern NFSv4.2 entry point. NFS14 is an optional, separately gated advanced followup. Use one shared fixture engine with named inputs, not every version×security×platform permutation. These IDs replace the earlier provisional NFS-01…NFS-12 backlog numbering; match by lesson title, not numeric position. Old AUTH_SYS-v4.0 and Kerberos-v4.0 entries are consolidated in NFS05; explicit nonjoined-client and connection-binding lessons are added.

Version and platform rules

ProfileActual distinctionCapability limit
NFSv3Separate MOUNTv3 path; AUTH_SYS and RPCSEC_GSS comparison.RFC1813 is Informational; RFC2623 supplies the Kerberos integration. Do not import historical DES examples.
NFSv4.0Integrated namespace and state; version-specific SETCLIENTID path.Required implementation support includes Kerberos krb5/krb5i/krb5p, but does not require selecting it for every mount.
NFSv4.1Sessions, slots and optional state protection.RFC8881: client krb5/krb5i MUST, client krb5p SHOULD; server krb5/krb5i/krb5p MUST. Distinguish required support from configured selection.
NFSv4.2 — defaultUse published RFC7862 with RFC8178; retain the v4.1 base machinery.NFSv4 minor version 2 does not itself turn on TLS, user authentication or optional v4.2 features.
Windows comparisonLinux client → Windows Server2025 NFSv4.1.Built-in Windows Client: v2/v3. Windows Server: v2/v3/v4.1 per current Microsoft table. No v4.2 or built-in v4.1 client claim.

The checked replacement work is rfc8881bis-11, 23 September2026, still an Internet-Draft. It does not replace published RFC8881 requirements. The contemporary TLS1.3 publication is RFC9846 (July2026), which obsoletes RFC8446. Recheck source status at implementation freeze; do not upgrade standards solely from draft wording.

Shared implementation contract

  • Profile metadata must name NFS major/minor version, RPCSEC_GSS version, selected sec service, mechanism/QOP/enctype, xprtsec, transport, state-protection policy, mapping adapter, authorization policy, source revisions and support evidence. A standards-based illustration is not a live interoperability badge.
  • The Linux model is pinned to the retrieved upstream manual snapshot and official kernel documentation, not an invented running build. Before any native-support badge, record actual kernel/config, nfs-utils, Kerberos library, optional gssproxy/tlshd/ktls-utils versions and one verified combination. Do not block offline core modeling on privileged native mounts.
  • Use stable objects for user/machine TGT and service ticket, local credential cache, service-key handle, GSS initiator/acceptor context and generation, sequence window, clientid, sessionid, slot request/cache, connection association, filehandle/stateid, identity map, export/file policy, TLS certificates/keys and exact packet instances. A handle is not a transferable bearer authorization.
  • Each network operation has send → receiver wire receipt → local decode/verification → accepted protocol effect. Sender knowledge of success waits for accepted response. Integrity-only content can be visible before verification but is not accepted; encrypted content cannot appear early. Check this in canonical holdings and every field/object replay.
  • Compute deterministic structural state: identities, operation order, XDR fields, service/tuple choices, sequence-window and slot decisions, exact references, policy outcomes and lifetimes. All crypto output remains SYM unless separately implemented against published numeric vectors. Label symbolic derivations as such; they are not proof of byte-level conformance.
  • Render protocol-defined local derivations and real decrypt/verify/use actions as replayable operations. Preserve genuine inspect-only context. Do not regress NET-05 by attaching encrypted packet fields only as glossary inspection entries.
  • Client initiator, server acceptor and KDC retain separate key custody. Server service keys and TLS private keys stay with their owners; GSS context handles never imply export of keys. Document the selected Kerberos context-key/subkey relation rather than simply copying a single session-key label everywhere.
  • Authentication outcome, effective authorization identity, export decision, file permission, operation result, and client acceptance are separate state paths. No server-generated response grants client knowledge before its verification event. Negative inputs stop at their first actual detector and retain unrelated accepted state.
  • For each added native operation/error, author an independent protocol worksheet with source section, legal operation placement, relevant status and detector before fixtures. Do not derive expected test outcomes from the scenario under test.

Teaching and navigation requirements

  • Expose Version, user authentication (sec), transport protection (xprtsec), client join state and effective server identity as separate beginner controls; show only supported combinations. Use plain outcomes such as “Alice authenticated; export is read-only”.
  • Provide a protection table for user assurance, host assurance, RPC-header integrity, body integrity/confidentiality and visible metadata. Retain exact endpoint/wire explanations in a deeper detail layer.
  • Keep at most five participants across a view. Expand kernel/helper/key-cache interactions locally; a mapping service is not a network participant unless the profile explicitly models and sources its query.
  • Version comparison links align discovery, caller proof, client/session state, request protection and permission checkpoints. Reuse prerequisites with an expand link without hiding the required actors/credentials.
  • Keyboard selection, field Replay path, exact-object history, rewind/reset and narrow viewport must preserve selected identity and canonical state. Add understandable labels for context handle versus sessionid versus filehandle/stateid.

Scenario manifest

IDLessonDelivery

NFS02Compare krb5, krb5i and krb5pmust-build core
