NFS01 — Modern default: authenticated private NFSv4.2 read

Goal: Follow one ordinary read from a credentialed client to an accepted result, keeping authentication and permission distinct.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2 minorversion2, sec=krb5p, xprtsec=none. RPCSEC_GSSv1; Kerberos GSS OID1.2.840.113554.1.2.2, QOP0; symbolic enctype19 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA256-128; mutual authentication; no delegation.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Fixed clock; Alice user TGT cached; separately provisioned machine credential; nfs/files.corp.example@CORP.EXAMPLE service key available only to the server/KDC.
  • Explicit export and a small named file policy fixture; v4.1 session bootstrap expanded via NFS06; delegations/pNFS off.

Required flow

  1. Show local desktop UID, selected user cache, and selected machine identity in separate cards.
  2. Request the nfs service ticket from the KDC; locally accept the TGS reply before making the ticket/context usable.
  3. Establish the RPCSEC_GSS context using INIT and any genuinely needed continuation; server acceptance and client verification of mutual proof are distinct.
  4. Complete supported client/session setup, then construct a minorversion2 user request for namespace traversal and OPEN.
  5. Send a krb5p READ; retain protected wire data at receipt; locally unwrap/verify and validate replay/state before policy evaluation.
  6. Evaluate mapped user, export and file policy; send the protected result; the client verifies it before displaying bytes. End with sourced CLOSE/context cleanup.

Named negative inputs

  • No user credential: stop at local context acquisition.
  • Invalid service-ticket key/version: reject context at the server.
  • Authenticated Alice lacks read permission: retain authentication success and deny file operation.
  • Corrupted protected result: client learns no file bytes.

Acceptance

  • Default catalog entry selects NFS01, not v3.
  • No file content at either receiving endpoint before the relevant verification/unwrap event.
  • TGT never sent to NFS server; service key never acquired by client.
  • minorversion2 adds no invented login handshake; no v4.0-only bootstrap operations appear.

Sources: N05, N06, N08, N10, N11, N12, L01, L04

NFS02 — Compare krb5, krb5i and krb5p

Goal: Compare the same READ at the same boundary under three independently scoped protection settings.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2; three fixed sec profiles; xprtsec=none. RPCSEC_GSSv1; Kerberos GSS OID1.2.840.113554.1.2.2, QOP0; symbolic enctype19 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA256-128; mutual authentication; no delegation.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Reuse accepted context setup as an expandable prerequisite, never as unexplained magic.
  • Each comparison run has its own context, sequence numbers and packet generation.

Required flow

  1. Present one protection map with RPC header, credential/verifier, procedure arguments and returned data as separate regions.
  2. Construct and verify the header MIC for each service; show none/integrity/privacy body treatments from the pinned RFC2203 worksheet.
  3. Run the same permitted READ through each receiver-local check.
  4. Display which fields remain visible to a network observer and which exact endpoint operation exposes protected content.

Named negative inputs

  • Alter a procedure argument under krb5: show the absence of a body-integrity guarantee, not a fabricated MIC rejection.
  • Alter an integrity-protected body: receiver rejects it.
  • Alter privacy ciphertext: unwrap fails.
  • Repeat an already-used GSS sequence: no second dispatch; use the specification-defined discard behavior.

Acceptance

  • Pseudo-flavor labels map to wire RPCSEC_GSS flavor6; no pseudo-flavor number is used as the RPC credential flavor.
  • Each displayed MIC has an explicit coverage list and source citation; do not claim whole IP/TCP encryption.
  • Corruption demonstrates the selected mode, not a blanket red failure for all modes.
  • At least header verifier, body and sequence number have exact operational field replay.

Sources: N08, N11, N12, L01

NFS03 — NFSv3: client-asserted identity and root squashing

Goal: Explain the separate mount path and the trust placed in client-supplied numeric identities.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv3/MOUNTv3; sec=sys; xprtsec=none; explicit root_squash, anonuid65534/anongid65534.

Actors: Local application; NFSv3 client; MOUNT service; NFS service and local filesystem policy

Preconditions

  • Configured export, fixed service endpoints and numeric identity namespace.
  • No KDC/context/certificate is implied; privileged-port policy, if displayed, is a separate fixture assumption.

Required flow

  1. Send MOUNTv3 MNT for the named export; local export decision produces filehandle and allowed auth flavors.
  2. Client receives the mount result; show that it is not a grant to read every file.
  3. Build NFSv3 LOOKUP/READ using AUTH_SYS stamp, machine-name, UID, primary GID and groups.
  4. At server receipt label the identity client asserted; perform configured squashing and file-policy checks.
  5. Return data or the sourced NFSv3 error; compare an ordinary caller with a UID/GID0 caller.

Named negative inputs

  • Export disallows client: mount denied.
  • UID0 maps to anonymous identity and file access is denied.
  • Same numeric UID names different people on two hosts: expose the namespace collision.
  • Forged client assertion is not magically detected cryptographically.

Acceptance

  • No v4 COMPOUND/session/stateid appears.
  • Root squash is visibly a mapping policy, not proof of user identity or a complete defense against all forged UIDs.
  • A filehandle possession test cannot bypass the file-policy evaluator.
  • All fields survive exact receipt/history inspection without being mislabeled verified credentials.

Sources: N01, N07, L02

NFS04 — NFSv3 can use Kerberos

Goal: Demonstrate that version3 is not synonymous with AUTH_SYS.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv3/MOUNTv3; sec=krb5i; xprtsec=none. RPCSEC_GSSv1; Kerberos GSS OID1.2.840.113554.1.2.2, QOP0; symbolic enctype19 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA256-128; mutual authentication; no delegation.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store; MOUNT service

Preconditions

  • NFS03 discovery skeleton, NFS service principal/key and valid user credentials.
  • Fixed MOUNT profile uses explicitly labeled AUTH_SYS discovery and advertises configured Kerberos pseudo-flavor; this discovery has no cryptographic integrity. The client pins krb5i as its minimum and never treats advertisement as proof.

Required flow

  1. Obtain the initial filehandle and flavor advertisement through the MOUNTv3 profile.
  2. Select krb5i by local policy; obtain/reuse an nfs service ticket and establish a mutual GSS context.
  3. Issue NFSv3 READ with RPCSEC_GSS header/body protection.
  4. Server verifies, maps and authorizes; client validates the response before using it.

Named negative inputs

  • MOUNT advertisement lacks a locally allowed flavor: no silent sys downgrade.
  • Wrong service target or failed mutual proof: no accepted context.
  • User ticket expires: context reacquisition follows the selected lifetime profile, not a KDC exchange per READ.

Acceptance

  • Align milestones with NFS03 and highlight only changed security portions.
  • Keep MOUNT success distinct from authenticated NFS data access.
  • No forwarding of the TGT/password; use flavor6 on the data RPC.

Sources: N01, N02, N08, N10, N11

NFS05 — NFSv4.0: integrated namespace and state

Goal: Explain what changed from v3 while avoiding a claim that v4 itself encrypts or authenticates users.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.0 minorversion0; default sec=krb5p, named sec=sys comparison; delegations off.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Version-specific operation worksheet; existing credential setup reused only for the Kerberos branch.
  • Explicitly configured server accepts the selected flavor.

Required flow

  1. Traverse the integrated namespace without a separate MOUNT RPC.
  2. For the secure branch, establish user GSS context and show separately scoped client-state identity.
  3. Use SETCLIENTID and SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM where required by the selected v4.0 trace, then OPEN/READ/CLOSE with version-correct state handling.
  4. Compare the AUTH_SYS branch at the same permission decision; render its identity assurance accurately.

Named negative inputs

  • Server policy refuses sys: stop at the sourced security boundary.
  • Missing client-state credential: fail setup, not Alice password validation.
  • Invalid/expired state input: show a state error independently of valid user authentication.

Acceptance

  • No EXCHANGE_ID, CREATE_SESSION or SEQUENCE in v4.0.
  • Keep GSS handle, clientid, filehandle and stateid visually distinct.
  • Capability-to-implement Kerberos is not narrated as mandatory selection on every mount.
  • A future delegation variant must separately source the callback direction; it is not silently included here.

Sources: N03, L01, L03

NFS06 — NFSv4.1: machine state and user access

Goal: Make machine protection of client/session state distinct from Alice’s file permissions.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.1 minorversion1; standards profile explicitly negotiates SP4_MACH_CRED with integrity protection and fixed must_enforce/must_allow bitmaps; no universal Linux-default claim.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Machine context and Alice context have separate identities and generations.
  • Server supports the selected state-protection option; the returned operation bitmap is fixed and displayed.

Required flow

  1. Establish the machine GSS context and submit EXCHANGE_ID; expand its selected protection policy.
  2. Accept the returned client identity only after checking the reply.
  3. Send CREATE_SESSION under the required identity; record accepted session and slot state.
  4. Create/reuse the separate user context and issue a SEQUENCE-prefixed OPEN/READ.
  5. Display machine-state permission and user-file permission side by side at the final decision.

Named negative inputs

  • Wrong machine principal tries protected maintenance: reject at that operation.
  • Valid machine context but missing Alice context: no Alice READ.
  • Unsupported protection selection: explicit negotiation failure, no silent downgrade.

Acceptance

  • Scripted tests exercise returned bitmap semantics instead of assuming every operation uses the machine credential.
  • No file permission is inferred from possession of clientid/sessionid.
  • Two users can have separate contexts on the modeled client; do not give one user the other’s cache.
  • Show RPC GSS sequence and NFS slot/sequence as different counters.

Sources: N04, L03, L04

NFS07 — Recover from a security-policy boundary

Goal: Show how a client discovers an acceptable security tuple without silently weakening local policy.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.1; fixed namespace crossing; SECINFO and supported SECINFO_NO_NAME; default krb5i to required krb5p.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • One export boundary with a fixed allowed tuple list; explicit client minimum protection.
  • No authentication policy selected solely from response order; source version-specific operation/error rules.

Required flow

  1. Issue the fixed namespace request under the insufficient tuple.
  2. Return NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC only at the worksheet’s legal operation boundary.
  3. Query SECINFO by component name; provide SECINFO_NO_NAME as a bounded alternate trace.
  4. Client evaluates mechanism OID/QOP/service and chooses an allowed tuple, then retries the operation.
  5. Complete the same user-mapping and file checks; security discovery alone grants nothing.

Named negative inputs

  • No common tuple satisfying local policy: stop denied.
  • Tampered unauthenticated discovery is not treated as proof; strict minimum remains enforced.
  • A following operation mistakenly uses a consumed filehandle: fail the fixture’s structural validation.

Acceptance

  • Tests assert actual operation/error pairs, not generic wrongsec text on READ.
  • The v4.1 SECINFO filehandle consumption difference is represented in state.
  • No mixed list of unmodeled flavors and no uncontrolled retry loop.
  • Tuple, policy minimum and final selection are inspectable and replayable where operational.

Sources: N04, N02, L01, L02

NFS08 — From principal to UID/GID to access decision

Goal: Explain why successful Kerberos authentication can still end in permission denial.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2/krb5p; explicit local principal map and filesystem adapter; named AUTH_SYS squash comparison.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Fixture declares principal→local-ID/group mapping and owner/owner_group display mapping separately.
  • Use a named synthetic permission model; distinguish Linux POSIX mode/ACL projection from the RFC NFSv4 ACE model rather than pretending they are identical.

Required flow

  1. Accept authenticated alice@CORP.EXAMPLE through the existing GSS helper.
  2. Resolve the configured authorization identity and groups locally; disclose the fixture mapping.
  3. Read owner/owner_group metadata and apply a separate display mapping.
  4. Evaluate export host/flavor/read-only rules, any configured squash mapping, and file authorization.
  5. Explain the first denying rule or permitted operation; return the appropriate protected result.

Named negative inputs

  • Unmapped authenticated principal follows the explicitly configured deny policy.
  • Owner-name display mapping fails while authenticated READ still succeeds.
  • Read-only export denies write; file ACL independently denies another operation.
  • Numeric identity collision or unauthorized group membership is visible, not corrected by inventing a KDC exchange.

Acceptance

  • Kerberos realm, DNS name, NFSv4 identity domain and local UID are separate fields.
  • Policy evidence lists the effective caller and first denying rule, without requiring the beginner to inspect JSON.
  • Root-squash/all-squash variants name their exact anonymous IDs and affected scope.
  • NFS ACCESS is a request-specific result, never an irrevocable future access token.

Sources: N14, L05, L02, N03

NFS09 — A non-domain-joined Linux workstation uses Kerberos

Goal: Answer how a locally logged-on user accesses a realm-protected NFS share without assuming domain join.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2/krb5p; MIT Kerberos1.22 documentation profile; manually provisioned realm configuration and host credential; no domain-join operation.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Local desktop identity workstation/alex differs from explicitly selected alice@CORP.EXAMPLE.
  • Reachable KDC, trustworthy service-name configuration, time alignment, mapped server account, and a separately provisioned machine keytab for this Linux v4 profile.
  • User cache location/type is supported by the chosen helper; no assumption that any arbitrary credential cache is discovered.

Required flow

  1. Show nonjoined state and manually configured realm/service mapping.
  2. Acquire Alice’s TGT through explicit kinit-style sign-in; cross-link the existing Kerberos AS lesson instead of reimplementing PKINIT/FAST here.
  3. Obtain the service ticket and initialize user GSS context.
  4. Show the separate machine credential required by the chosen client-state path, then resume NFS01.
  5. Server authenticates the selected realm principal and checks its own mapping/export/file policy.

Named negative inputs

  • User TGT exists but required machine keytab is absent: stop at machine/state setup.
  • Local UID maps to a different credential cache: no implicit use of Alice’s ticket.
  • Wrong realm/service name or KDC unreachable: credential acquisition failure.
  • Authentication succeeds but mapping or file policy denies access.

Acceptance

  • The result says join is not the protocol proof; it does not say kinit always suffices.
  • No join-derived trust or SPN registration is silently fabricated.
  • No claim rpc.gssd -n removes machine-state credential requirements.
  • A compact v3 comparison may omit v4 state requirements, but is not an escape hatch presented as a universal modern setup.

Sources: K01, K02, L03, N10, N14

NFS10 — Add a connection without inventing a new user login

Goal: Separate NFS session binding and replay control from authentication and filesystem authorization.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.1/4.2 standards profile; one server, two TCP connections; SP4_MACH_CRED requires BIND_CONN_TO_SESSION in returned must_enforce bitmap; no pNFS/trunking topology expansion.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Accepted NFS06 session and fixed state-protection policy; same server identity verified by the profile.
  • Existing user GSS context and a deterministic outstanding request/slot fixture.

Required flow

  1. Open a second connection and bind it using the required protected machine context.
  2. Server checks binding conditions before associating it with the existing session; client verifies the response before marking connection usable.
  3. Send an ordinary user request through the added connection; apply user authorization as before.
  4. Demonstrate a lost response and permitted session replay using a fresh acceptable GSS RPC sequence with the same NFS slot request.

Named negative inputs

  • Possession of sessionid without required proof does not bind a connection.
  • Wrong principal or invalid proof fails before connection usability.
  • Replayed GSS sequence is rejected/discarded by GSS handling; a distinct valid session retry returns the recorded result.
  • One connection fails: display surviving session state only where the selected trace permits it.

Acceptance

  • No copied SMB binding flags, SMB signing keys or automatic KDC exchange per connection.
  • Test no duplicate application side effect and no privilege gain.
  • Failed binding does not manufacture usable connection state.
  • Name NFS session binding, GSS/TLS channel binding and TLS session as three distinct concepts.

Sources: N04, N08, L01

NFS11 — RPC-with-TLS protects a transport, not a user claim

Goal: Explain server-only versus mutual host authentication while preserving AUTH_SYS’s identity limits.

Profile: NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2/TCP; sec=sys; default xprtsec=mtls, named tls comparison; TLS1.3 RFC9846; TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, X25519, ECDSA P-256 certificate signatures (ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256), no resumption/0-RTT.

Actors: Local users on one client; Client RPC/TLS endpoint; Server RPC/TLS endpoint and export policy; Local certificate/trust stores

Preconditions

  • TLS helper configured, explicit trust and host authorization policy.
  • Visible server/client certificate identities; different endpoint private-key handles.
  • Apply the ALPN discrepancy disposition in the source notes before coding the wire flight.

Required flow

  1. Use the RPC NULL procedure with empty AUTH_TLS credential and empty AUTH_NONE verifier. Accept only MSG_ACCEPTED with an AUTH_NONE verifier containing the eight ASCII octets STARTTLS; then start TLS on that same TCP connection. The probe accept_stat is not itself the TLS-support criterion.
  2. Perform TLS1.3, including the server request for a client identity; tls may accept no client certificate, mtls requires the selected valid identity.
  3. Separate certificate receipt, local handshake-key derivation/decryption, certificate/proof validation and established transport.
  4. Carry AUTH_SYS RPC in application-data ciphertext, followed by receiver-local decoded RPC.
  5. Show two client user IDs on the same host transport; apply export/squash/file policy independently for each.

Named negative inputs

  • Client certificate absent in required-mtls profile: transport not admitted.
  • Valid client certificate but host unauthorized: no accepted association.
  • Valid TLS with forged UID: no invented user-identity proof.
  • Corrupted application-data record: no decoded RPC or file effect.

Acceptance

  • Only outer TLS record is visible on wire; decoded RPC appears at the receiver’s actual decrypt event.
  • No HTTPS wrapping or separate invented NFS-TLS port.
  • Each endpoint derives its own directional traffic-secret objects; private keys never move.
  • TLS-only and mTLS badges describe hosts; sec=sys remains client-asserted user identity.

Sources: N15, N16, N17, L01, L02, N07

NFS12 — Required transport protection fails closed

Goal: Locate failures before NFS access rather than misreporting them as a user-password error.

Profile: NFS-TLS-STRICT-R1, revision2026-10-21. Reuse NFS11 TLS profile with fixed xprtsec=mtls and no cleartext fallback.

Actors: Client RPC/TLS endpoint; Server RPC/TLS endpoint; Local trust and policy stores

Preconditions

  • A single failure input changes one condition; retain the same declared protection policy.
  • Certificate validation includes the chosen identity/use/time/revocation policy; offline revocation outcomes are synthetic, not live OCSP claims.

Required flow

  1. Attempt the NFS11 discovery/handshake until the selected failure detector.
  2. Record the actual failing protocol/local-policy stage and the client’s observation.
  3. Stop the selected connection/mount attempt; keep the request undispatched and application data unavailable.
  4. Show a concise repair hint tied to that cause; an opportunistic comparison, if displayed, is a separate explicitly labeled policy.

Named negative inputs

  • Unsupported/malformed AUTH_TLS reply: do not send ClientHello.
  • Wrong server name or untrusted/expired certificate: validation fails.
  • Missing/incompatible sunrpc ALPN: no accepted RPC transport.
  • mTLS-required client identity missing or invalid; selected revocation check rejects.

Acceptance

  • No cleartext retry under strict policy.
  • No phantom GSS failure or NFS wrong-password error.
  • Client-side failure knowledge follows actual response/local validation; no instantaneous shared global status.
  • Retry/reset cannot reuse rejected transport keys as an established channel.

Sources: N15, N16, N17, L01

NFS13 — Linux client to Windows Server for NFS

Goal: Show the supported Windows server comparison without claiming nonexistent built-in client capabilities.

Profile: NFS-WINDOWS2025-R1, revision2026-10-21. Windows Server2025 Server for NFS, Linux client, NFSv4.1/TCP sec=krb5p; enctype17 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96; explicit AD lookup configuration. Documentation-backed model, no native build verification.

Actors: Linux user/client; AD DS KDC; Windows Server2025 Server for NFS; Configured mapping/share/filesystem policy

Preconditions

  • NFS server role, service principal/key provisioning and permitted share documented explicitly.
  • AD lookup selected; account mapping fixture pinned. Do not animate unsupported internal LDAP/LSA call chains.

Required flow

  1. Display the vendor support table before the flow.
  2. Acquire the nfs service ticket from AD and establish the mutual RPCSEC_GSS context.
  3. Perform the v4.1 namespace/session request using the documented security flavor.
  4. Resolve the explicit server authorization identity and evaluate NFS share policy plus filesystem access.
  5. Return the protected read or distinct mapping/policy denial; verify at the client.

Named negative inputs

  • Built-in Windows Client for NFS selected with v4.1: unsupported-profile explanation, not simulated success.
  • Windows server v4.2 selected: unsupported by the cited capability table.
  • Service-key mismatch, mapping failure and ACL denial produce different local decision states.

Acceptance

  • Table says Server v2/v3/v4.1; built-in Client v2/v3; no inferred v4.0/v4.2 support.
  • Current Server docs’ krb5/krb5i/krb5p support overrides older restricted blog claims; version labels remain explicit.
  • No assumed RFC8009 enctype19 interoperability with Windows and no RC4/DES fallback.
  • No domain-controller request fabricated on every READ; local mapping adapter exposes its scope and limits.

Sources: W01, W02, W03, W04, N04, N10, N11, N13

Optional extension — outside core completion

NFS14 — Advanced: bind user GSS authentication to TLS

Goal: Keep host transport authentication and user GSS authentication distinct, with an explicit binding check.

Profile: NFS-GSS-TLS-STANDARDS-R1, revision2026-10-21. Standards-only followup; one user GSS mechanism instance on one TLS1.3 connection; implementation support unverified.

Actors: Local user/application; Linux NFS client and credential helper; KDC; NFS server with local policy store

Preconditions

  • Source-confirm and pin the exact RPCSEC_GSS/channel-binding profile before implementation; do not call a generic Linux sec=krb5 mount a verified binding implementation.
  • Use a single GSS context per teaching transport; no multiuser shared-binding generalization.

Required flow

  1. Finish the NFS11 TLS handshake and locally derive tls-exporter binding data at each endpoint.
  2. Use RFC9266 exporter label EXPORTER-Channel-Binding, zero-length context and 32-byte output; label the result binding data, not an application encryption key.
  3. Establish the user GSS context with the pinned binding interface and demonstrate endpoint comparison.
  4. Carry the selected RPC protection inside TLS; authorization still uses the authenticated user.
  5. End the upper-layer exchange and close the teaching connection; do not reuse the binding for another mechanism instance.

Named negative inputs

  • Different TLS connection supplies different binding: reject before usable user context.
  • TLS valid but GSS user proof invalid: retain transport success, deny user authentication.
  • Selected implementation lacks required binding interface: unsupported capability, not a silently weakened success.

Acceptance

  • Evidence includes the exact implementation or a conspicuous standards-only badge.
  • TLS traffic secrets, binding value and GSS context keys are distinct objects.
  • RFC9266 section4.1 instance/lifetime restrictions are explicitly checked.
  • No universal RPCSEC_GSSv3, Linux or Windows support claim.

Sources: N15, N18, N09, N11, L04

Implementation order and release evidence

  1. Freeze source ledger and author the independent field/operation/permission worksheets. Implement shared inventory/state helpers and NFS01/02/08 first; verify one full receiver acceptance path before adding comparisons.
  2. Add NFS03–07 and NFS09–10 using bounded named inputs. Preserve minor-version operation constraints and identity boundaries. Add NFS11–13 only after the transport and vendor-profile notes are explicit.
  3. For every core default and named negative: record sourceIndex, wire/decoded/exact representations, principal, key/context generation, first detector, effect count, client knowledge and cleanup. Assert replay/seek/reset equivalence and noninterference across scenarios.
  4. Mount the actual app and select/replay at least: AUTH_SYS UID, GSS context handle, header verifier, protected body, mapped identity, SECINFO service, session slot, TLS record/decoded RPC, and Windows result. Compare final canonical state with the full-source prefix. Test genuine inspect context remains unplayable.
  5. Use representative native UI acceptance in source HTTP, standalone HTTP and standalone file, at desktop/narrow widths and required keyboard paths. Rebuild a self-contained artifact; record its bytes/hash and evidence against that exact candidate. Preserve baseline coverage and run the parent project’s required regression gates.
  6. Deliver a manifest mapping each NFS ID/variant to profile/source worksheet/tests and clear implemented/illustrated/not-tested capabilities. No broad “RFC certified” or all-platform interoperability claim; document actual remaining limits.

Source caveats and bounded followups

  • RPC9289 section5 says server ALPN appears in ServerHello, while current TLS1.3/IANA place ALPN in EncryptedExtensions. Model TLS1.3 correctly: ClientHello offer and encrypted server EncryptedExtensions selection sunrpc. Record this source discrepancy; do not call it a verified erratum. The RFC Editor errata endpoint was inaccessible on2026-10-21. The worker must recheck it and record the actual disposition at source freeze; absence of an errata result is not proof none exists.
  • RFC9266 section4.1 restricts reuse of tls-exporter binding across authentication mechanism instances. NFS14 deliberately uses one user/context and closes its teaching connection. A multiuser combined GSS/TLS implementation needs a separately sourced binding design; do not infer it from ordinary Linux mount options.
  • The official kernel GSS page says RPCSEC_GSSv3 is not implemented. Keep Full Mode Labeled NFS, multi-principal/subject-label assertions and advanced GSSv3 delegation as standards-only research until a named implementation proves support.
  • Retain Labeled NFS, inter-server COPY/delegation and pNFS data-server authorization as bounded later work, not fourteen more permutations. Each requires its own selected feature/layout/mode, source worksheet, extra actors and implementation evidence. Limited Server label storage is not Full Mode MAC enforcement; a layout is not universal user authorization at a data server.
  • NFS multi-domain identity mapping is not synonymous with AD forest trust. A later cross-realm variant must connect the existing Kerberos referral lesson to an explicit remote principal mapping and local permission decision; it must not assume numeric UID compatibility across administrative domains.

Windows workstation logon and elevation

14 core scenarios WLOG01–08 and WELEV01–06; optional WELEV07. Existing ADDS crypto, SMB3.1.1, RDP and WinRM lessons are reused/cross-linked, not rewritten.

Pinned profiles

  • Windows11 supported Enterprise/Pro workstation reference with exact build/servicing date recorded before product-specific claims; ADDS Server2025 target where applicable. No implicit Entra join, Microsoft account, consumer Hello or automatic sign-in.
  • Classic UAC examples explicitly select classic Admin Approval Mode and a non-built-in administrator. Administrator protection is a separate current feature with an evidence gate.
  • Credential Guard state must be recorded: keep opaque LSA credential handles by default; if enabled, represent LSAIso/VBS custody without claiming every secret is plaintext in LSASS. Cached-verifier, local-SAM and service-ticket limits remain distinct.

Implementation contract

  • Use local-call/local-check/local-create events for Winlogon, LSA, SAM, token and AppInfo operations. Do not turn local OS API calls into network packets or describe every such operation as RFC protocol traffic.
  • Separate credential collection, validation, local logon eligibility, token creation, process creation, profile/desktop readiness, resource access and the user learning a result.
  • Every token has owner/logon-context/primary-or-impersonation type, user SID, attributed group SIDs, privileges plus enabled flags, integrity/elevation metadata and lifecycle; token copies are not independent authenticated users.
  • Keep raw input, account verifier, cached verifier, certificate/private-key handle, Kerberos credential and token as different artifacts. Permission to inspect is not possession.
  • Group/PAC information is attributable to its authority; local policy/alias additions are separate. Do not imply every unlock/elevation refreshes all existing tokens.
  • Author source/protection/decoded-acceptance events and cleanup/release histories for every readable result. Never give an observer future server/DC knowledge at request or wire receipt.
  • Diagram logical LSA/authentication-package/SAM/token roles within the same workstation with parent grouping. Keep no more than five horizontal actors; group or split a detailed stage.

Usability and teaching boundaries

  • At all times show: device membership, console account authority, local process SID/account, outbound identity, effective logon/elevation policy, and current authentication-versus-authorization decision.
  • Offer explicit local/domain and classic/Administrator-protection profile selectors before playback, with a textual explanation of what changes. Profile choice resets history rather than mutating a running principal.
  • Provide token comparison tables and simple labels: credential verified, console allowed, token created, desktop ready, resource allowed. Separate consent, credential verification, local PIN entry and network authentication.
  • Cross-link exact accepted SMB/AD scenario IDs and retain return-to-origin context; avoid duplicating catalog entries that merely restate an existing protocol flow.

Research and evidence gates

  • Before code, capture relevant official page/spec bytes, final URL, revision/build scope, retrieval date and SHA256 under the listed snapshotReference paths; sourceSnapshotStatus must remain pending until bytes exist.
  • Pin MS-KILE/MS-PAC current versions and revalidate the existing AD03/AD04 Windows profile gates. Do not copy older weak mapping, SHA1/RSA-transport or universal fallback claims from broad legacy articles.
  • Resolve current Administrator-protection support-label discrepancy. Offline smart-card and WHfB detailed flows are named research branches, not silently omitted promises or fabricated implementations.
  • For declared product support, record Windows edition/build, DC build, effective policies, token inspection and narrowly scoped logs/traces. Synthetic tests establish authored-model consistency, not interoperability.

WLOG01 — Workgroup workstation: local password logon

Follow a local account from credential collection through SAM validation, interactive-logon authorization and a usable desktop; show where an access token first exists.

Actors: U: user; L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider; A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role; P: user process/session and kernel token role; S: local SAM authority

Preconditions

  • Windows11 supported Enterprise/Pro reference; workgroup PC WORKGROUPPC; LOCAL bob is a standard user.
  • Password provider; no domain, cloud account, Hello or automatic sign-in; local policy permits console logon.

Required event sequence

  1. collect · local-input · U → L: Select WORKGROUPPC\bob and enter the synthetic password. Credential collection is not authentication. Boundary: No authenticated identity or token yet. Artifacts: account-scope, credential-input-buffer.
  2. submit · local-call · L → A: Submit the declared interactive-logon request and selected authentication package. Boundary: Local IPC, never an HTTP/NTLM challenge exchange. Artifacts: interactive-logon-request.
  3. verify · local-call · A → S: The local package validates the submitted credential against the SAM account authority and returns account/group data. Boundary: Only S/A learn verification success at their actual boundaries. Artifacts: local-account-verifier, validation-result.
  4. authorize · local-check · A → A: Evaluate console logon rights and account restrictions, then form the new logon session and primary token. Boundary: Authentication alone does not bypass an explicit deny right. Artifacts: local-logon-policy, logon-LUID, primary-token.
  5. desktop · local-create · A → P: Attach the token to userinit/shell startup, load the selected profile, then mark desktop ready. Boundary: Token availability precedes successful profile/desktop startup. Artifacts: primary-token, profile, desktop-session.
  6. access · local-check · P → P: Evaluate one declared file DACL with this token; record grant separately from sign-in. Boundary: A signed-in user can still be denied a file. Artifacts: file-security-descriptor, access-decision.

Negative and failure variants

Variant / detectorCondition and stopping pointState preserved
bad-password / SLocal verifier mismatch; stop at verifyNo token/desktop; no DC traffic.
disabled-account / SSelected account disabled; stop at verifyNo success result.
deny-interactive / ASeDenyInteractiveLogonRight applies despite valid password; stop at authorizeCredential verification remains historical; no successful console session.
profile-failure / PProfile startup fails after token creation; stop at desktopAuthentication history remains; desktopReady=false.

Acceptance

  • Every named actor/store is local; zero network messages in this profile.
  • Token contains a synthetic local user SID, attributed group SIDs, privilege list with enabled flags, logon identifier and integrity label; no password or Kerberos ticket embedded.
  • Credential-input buffers receive a declared cleanup event; durable verifier and token have different owners/lifetimes.
  • No token exists at credential receipt or before authority/policy checks.

Held artifacts: local account/verifier; credential input buffer; local policy; validation result; logon LUID; primary token; profile; desktop session; file DACL/decision

Primary sources: W-S01, W-S02, W-S03, W-S06, W-S07

WLOG02 — Domain-member workstation: online AD DS password logon

Connect local Windows sign-in to actual Kerberos AS/TGS work, local workstation service-ticket validation, and locally created access tokens.

Actors: U: user; L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider; A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role; P: user process/session and kernel token role; K: AD DS KDC/account database; M: workstation machine credential and local Kerberos acceptor

Preconditions

  • WORKSTATION is an ADDS member; CORP\alice exists; DC/DNS/time and machine relationship work.
  • Select AES password preauthentication; no NTLM fallback in this fixture; FAST disabled only to isolate WLOG06.
  • Pin current supported Windows11 client, Server2025 KDC, policy and complete MS-KILE revision; logical roles are not separate external servers.

Required event sequence

  1. input · local-input · U → L: Collect explicitly scoped CORP\alice input and submit to the local Kerberos authentication package. Boundary: LSASS submission is not a network request. Artifacts: credential-input, logon-request.
  2. as · network-exchange · A → K: Run existing AS request/reply model, including selected preauth metadata, client-derived key and KDC-owned authoritative key. Boundary: No clear password crosses the KDC leg. Artifacts: AS-REQ, AS-REP, user-account-key, KDC-user-key, opaque-TGT.
  3. as-accept · local-verify · A → A: Decrypt and validate the client part before acquiring the issued TGT session key and installing the opaque TGT. Boundary: Ticket receipt is distinct from usable credential acquisition. Artifacts: accepted-TGT-credential.
  4. host-ticket · network-exchange · A → K: Request host/workstation.corp.example for the workstation itself and validate its TGS reply. Boundary: Do not stop the sign-in explanation at receiving a TGT. Artifacts: host-TGS-REQ, host-ticket, host-session-key.
  5. local-ticket-check · local-call · A → M: The workstation Kerberos runtime interprets its host ticket and validated authorization data using its own service identity. Boundary: This is local workstation processing, not a fabricated network AP exchange to another host. Artifacts: host-ticket, validated-logon-information.
  6. token · local-create · A → P: Combine validated domain identity/group information with local policy/alias membership and logon rights; create the primary token and start the session. Boundary: Token issued locally, not sent by KDC. Artifacts: domain-SID, group-SID-set, local-policy, primary-token, desktop-session.
  7. network-boundary · teaching-link · P → P: Offer a separate network-resource lesson using the retained credential context. Boundary: Desktop success does not authorize a share/file. Artifacts: credential-context-reference.

Negative and failure variants

Variant / detectorCondition and stopping pointState preserved
wrong-password / KPreauthentication fails; stop at asNo accepted user TGT or local token.
clock-or-spn / K/ATime or workstation service target invalid; stop at as or host-ticketNo invented local success; retain prior valid credential history where applicable.
host-key-mismatch / MTicket cannot be accepted by the selected machine identity; stop at local-ticket-checkTGT receipt is not a desktop grant.
denied-local-logon / ADomain authentication succeeds but local deny right applies; stop at tokenNo usable desktop; no arbitrary cached bypass.
password-change-required / KAccount requires change before authentication completes; stop at asExplicit stop/cross-link; do not invent an inline password-change protocol.

Acceptance

  • Assert AS/TGS target, key owner, reply receipt/acceptance and local-token boundaries.
  • No domain password transmitted to SAM, no SAM verifier masquerading as an AES key, and no user token copied out of a TGT.
  • Token provenance lists domain identity/group facts separately from local aliases/privileges and application access decisions.
  • Do not teach arbitrary Kerberos-error-to-NTLM fallback; a future compatibility branch needs its own sourced condition and carrier.

Held artifacts: user/KDC AES handles; AS client part/TGT/TGT key; host ticket/key; validated PAC/logon data; local group/policy facts; token; profile/session

Cross-links: Existing standalone ADDS/password lessons; lab-smb-nonjoined-kerberos

Primary sources: W-S05, W-S02, W-S06, W-S28

WLOG03 — Domain member, explicit local account: same name, different SID

Explain why .\alice, WORKSTATION\alice and CORP\alice can select different authorities and do not become the same principal because their names match.

Actors: U: user; L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider; A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role; P: user process/session and kernel token role; S: local SAM authority; K: ADDS authority shown as uncontacted

Preconditions

  • Machine is a domain member; both local alice and domain alice exist with deliberately different SIDs/password fixtures.

  3. token · local-create · A → P: Authorize local logon and create a token with the machine-local SID. Boundary: No CORP SID or domain TGT is inferred. Artifacts: local-token.
  4. compare · local-check · P → P: Run a selected local ACL check and show the different result for the hypothetical CORP SID without changing this process identity. Boundary: Comparison does not transfer another principal token. Artifacts: local-ACL, access-decision.
  5. network · teaching-link · P → P: Cross-link explicit domain network credentials while retaining this desktop identity. Boundary: Network credential entry is a later independent action. Artifacts: local-token-reference.

WELEV06 — Windows11 Administrator protection: isolated elevation context

Contrast a policy-pinned Administrator-protection elevation with classic split-token UAC, without inventing Windows Hello credential internals.

Actors: U: signed-in administrator; P: deprivileged process; B/L: platform elevation broker/verification UI; A: system-managed administrator identity/profile; E: isolated elevated process

Preconditions

  • Research gate: pin exact supported build/update/edition and effective Administrator-protection policy; do not call it universal Windows11 behavior.
  • Select one documented prompt policy and an OS verification-result boundary; Hello/PIN/password internals stay explicitly abstract unless separately sourced.

Required event sequence

  1. initial · local-inspect · P → P: Show the normal process deprivileged state and effective feature policy. Boundary: Do not seed a reusable classic full-token pair as the explanation. Artifacts: deprivileged-token, feature-policy.
  2. request · local-call · P → B/L: Submit the concrete elevated operation and invoke the configured verification/approval experience. Boundary: Prompt policy is explicit, not inferred from generic branding. Artifacts: elevation-request, verification-prompt.
  3. verify · platform-boundary · U → B/L: Complete the selected OS identity-verification/approval contract. Boundary: No invented PIN-to-KDC or biometric network exchange. Artifacts: verification-result.
  4. isolate · local-create · B/L → A: Use the system-managed separate administrator context/profile to create the isolated elevated token. Boundary: Source attribution stays at the documented architectural level. Artifacts: system-managed-identity, isolated-admin-token, separate-profile.
  5. launch · local-create · A → E: Launch the requested elevated operation, preserving P and separating profile/credential context. Boundary: Do not copy standard-session domain/cloud SSO credentials by assumption. Artifacts: E, isolated-token-reference.
  6. end · local-cleanup · E → A: End the chosen isolated process/context and release its elevation token; later elevation requires another authorized lifecycle. Boundary: Record child/reference semantics from the pinned implementation if modeled. Artifacts: token-release.

Negative and failure variants

Variant / detectorCondition and stopping pointState preserved
cancel-or-fail / B/LVerification cancelled or rejected; stop at verifyNo isolated elevated process.
unsupported-build / B/LFeature/policy unavailable on chosen build; stop at initialHonest unsupported profile, not classic behavior mislabeled.
separate-profile-access / ERequired user-profile data/SSO unavailable in isolated context; stop at launchElevation is not proof of reusable network credentials.
policy-mode-mismatch / B/LClassic mode selected instead; stop at initialRoute to WELEV01/02 without rebranding classic tokens.

Acceptance

  • Show effective policy and source support status beside the lesson.
  • No claim Administrator protection is enabled by default on all Windows11 installations: baseline-managed and general defaults differ.
  • Do not model Hello PIN as an AD password, remote credential or generic PKINIT message.
  • If build/support gate cannot be resolved, deliver clearly labeled architectural reference plus an exact research disposition; no false native-tested badge.

Held artifacts: feature/prompt policy; verification result; system-managed identity; isolated token/profile; process; release

Cross-links: WELEV01; WELEV02

Additional research gate:

  • Reconcile 2026-10-13 landing-page availability/October-baseline text with CSP Insider Preview11.0.26100.9278 applicability. Capture chosen KB/build/policy and native observations before product-support claims.
  • WHfB key trust, certificate trust and cloud trust are distinct mechanisms; do not graft an unsourced universal PIN flow onto this scenario.

WELEV07 — Optional: sudo for Windows delegates elevation to UAC

Explain the Windows command’s UAC-backed elevation and console modes without importing Unix sudoers/PAM semantics.

Actors: U: console user; P: unelevated sudo client; B: UAC/elevation service; E: elevated command

Preconditions

  • Optional follow-on after WELEV01–06; pin Windows11 24H2+ build and sudo version.
  • Feature explicitly enabled; choose forceNewWindow for the base; named disableInput/normal modes only if demonstrated.

Required event sequence

  1. invoke · local-input · U → P: Enter a harmless predefined sudo command. Boundary: No Unix policy file or timestamp cache is invented. Artifacts: command, sudo-mode.
  2. uac · local-call · P → B: Request platform UAC elevation using the effective Windows policy. Boundary: Windows sudo is not a replacement authentication protocol. Artifacts: elevation-request.
  3. approve · local-input · U → B: Complete the actual configured UAC prompt. Boundary: Cancel produces no elevated command. Artifacts: approval-result.
  4. launch · local-create · B → E: Start the command in the selected window/input mode with its accepted elevated context. Boundary: Changing console mode does not select an alternate account. Artifacts: process, token-reference, stdio-mode.
  5. exit · local-result · E → P: Return/close the selected command and release scoped handles. Boundary: No persistent general-purpose admin grant. Artifacts: exit-status.

Negative and failure variants

Variant / detectorCondition and stopping pointState preserved
disabled / Psudo feature not enabled; stop at invokeNo implicit configuration change.
uac-cancel / BPrompt declined; stop at approveNo elevated command.
other-user-option / PUnsupported attempt to run as another user; stop at invokeCross-link runas; do not pretend sudo -u compatibility.

Acceptance

  • Label Windows sudo distinctly from Linux/macOS sudo lessons.
  • forceNewWindow, disableInput and normal affect I/O coupling, not PAM/sudoers policy.
  • Do not include this optional scenario in mandatory core acceptance count unless selected by root plan.

Held artifacts: command/mode; UAC request/result; elevated process/token; I/O handles; exit status

Cross-links: WELEV02; WELEV04

Cover wrong-password /netonly launch, cached/no-cache split, same-name SID separation, DC-required unlock, consent-vs-credentials, UAC cancellation, and all key custody transitions reused from AD.
  • Add field/held-object replay for token creation/consumption/release and protected-result acceptance. For WIN-11 cleanup, author H-local acceptor-subkey creation in six fixed/seven derived raw-CredSSP/RDP profiles without adding the secret to wire objects. Keep its P3 scope separate and do not reopen accepted WIN01–10.
