MCP01 — Remote MCP: discovery to authorized tool result

Follow one complete human-delegated request, identifying who issues the token and who finally decides to run the tool.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core MCP 2026-07-28 HTTP authorization teaching profile; authorization itself is optional for MCP deployments. No deprecated session or DCR default.

Actors: Host / MCP client C; User and browser B; Protected MCP resource R; Authorization server A.

Declared setup

  • MCP 2026-07-28 over HTTPS Streamable HTTP; canonical resource https://mcp.lab.example/team/mcp.
  • Public desktop client is already registered at A; redirect is an approved loopback callback, no embedded client secret.
  • A advertises S256; lab scope files:read is illustrative, not a standardized MCP-wide scope.

Authored sequence

  1. C sends a self-contained tools/list POST with correct current-version metadata but no token; R returns 401 with Bearer resource_metadata and files:read guidance.
  2. C obtains and validates resource metadata, selects A, then separately obtains validated A metadata. Label discovery as configuration discovery, not authentication success.
  3. C creates per-attempt state, verifier and S256 challenge; B carries the authorization request with resource and requested scope to A.
  4. A performs its chosen user authentication and consent; depict those as A-owned local/interaction steps, not an MCP password exchange.
  5. B returns a short-lived code. C checks transaction/issuer/redirect binding, then sends grant_type=authorization_code, client_id, code, verifier and resource to the recorded token endpoint.
  6. After A validates the grant, C acquires an access token; C sends it in Authorization on the retried POST.
  7. R separately recovers, validates and authorizes the request; then returns a tool list. A later approved read tool call returns a result only after its own policy decision.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • User cancels consent: no token or tool execution.
  • Missing token on a later POST: challenge again; an earlier successful request grants no connection-wide authority.
  • No advertised PKCE capability: stop before opening the authorization flow.

Acceptance

  • Show token receipt before R validation and validation before tool execution.
  • Verifier never appears in browser authorization parameters or at R.
  • Resource parameter is visible on both authorization and token requests; access token is absent from URLs.
  • Full and filtered replay converge on the same accepted-result state.

Primary references: User-requested tutorial, MCP authorization 2026-07-28, RFC 9728 — Protected Resource Metadata, RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators, RFC 7636 — PKCE, RFC 6750 — Bearer use, MCP Streamable HTTP 2026-07-28.

MCP02 — Discover the correct resource and authorization server

Make challenge precedence, path-aware discovery and issuer-isolated credentials observable before any secret is sent.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core MCP 2026-07-28 HTTP authorization teaching profile; authorization itself is optional for MCP deployments. No deprecated session or DCR default.

Actors: MCP client C; Protected resource R; Authorization servers A and A2.

Declared setup

  • Resource path is /team/mcp; authorization issuer is https://login.lab.example/tenant-a.
  • Two metadata variants: explicit challenge pointer; no pointer with well-known fallback.
  • A2 is a separately configured issuer, not an alias of A.

Authored sequence

  1. Parse WWW-Authenticate; prefer its resource_metadata URI when present.
  2. Without a pointer, try the path-specific protected-resource well-known URI, then its root fallback; show both exact requests and outcomes.
  3. Validate the recovered resource identifier before using authorization_servers; select one issuer under the profile policy.
  4. For a path-bearing issuer, try OAuth metadata path insertion, OIDC path insertion, then OIDC path appending in the MCP-defined order.
  5. Check metadata issuer equality; bind selected endpoints/capabilities to the same issuer record.
  6. Change resource metadata from A to A2. Keep existing A credentials/tokens isolated; obtain applicable A2 registration rather than forwarding A secrets. CIMD URL portability does not make A tokens portable.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Mismatched resource or issuer: metadata is unusable and no credential request follows.
  • All permitted discovery endpoints fail: explain the missing document instead of inventing /authorize or /token.
  • A valid JSON document without required authorization-server information is rejected.
  • A2 receives neither A refresh token nor A client secret.

Acceptance

  • Inspector distinguishes received JSON, validated metadata and selected issuer.
  • Record the actual attempted URLs and exact reason for fallback.
  • Header presence has precedence; tests include multiple challenges and quoted parameter parsing.
  • Resource canonicalization and issuer exact comparison are separate operations.

Primary references: MCP authorization-server discovery 2026-07-28, RFC 9728 — Protected Resource Metadata, RFC 8414 — Authorization Server Metadata, OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, errata set 2, MCP client registration 2026-07-28.

MCP03 — Registration choices: CIMD and existing client registration

Explain how a client becomes known to an authorization server without suggesting that registration grants resource access.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core HTTP authorization registration choices: issuer-specific pre-registration or advertised CIMD. RFC7591 DCR is deprecated MCP compatibility only, never the default or a universal requirement.

Actors: MCP client C; Authorization server A; Client metadata host M; User configuring client.

Declared setup

  • CIMD profile uses an HTTPS client_id with a nonempty path and A advertises client_id_metadata_document_supported.
  • Sibling profile has a valid pre-registered client ID at the same issuer.
  • DCR is available only as a visibly labeled compatibility variant, with registration_endpoint explicitly advertised.

Authored sequence

  1. Apply the declared choice order: usable existing registration first; otherwise advertised CIMD.
  2. For CIMD, A obtains a synthetic metadata document from the client_id URL, validates required members and exact client_id identity, and checks the requested redirect against that document.
  3. A records the allowed redirect/client authentication method; show that this is registration trust, not proof that a particular user approved access.
  4. Resume MCP01 with the established client ID and a fresh authorization transaction.
  5. Compatibility comparison: when explicitly selected and supported, display RFC7591 request/response, application_type and registration failure handling; never make DCR the default.
  6. If no supported mechanism or configured registration exists, stop with a useful configuration action; do not fabricate credentials.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • CIMD client_id differs from its document URL.
  • Requested redirect absent from metadata, malformed JSON, unavailable document or disallowed trust domain.
  • Public client incorrectly configured to rely on a packaged secret.
  • DCR compatibility branch uses incompatible native/web redirect rules or registration fails.

Acceptance

  • CIMD is labeled draft-based and DCR deprecated compatibility for this MCP revision.
  • A registration object and later consent/grant objects have different exact IDs and authority states.
  • Client names/logos are untrusted display metadata; approval UI identifies redirect hostname.
  • Registration choice/retry preserves focus and clearly exposes why setup cannot continue.

Primary references: MCP client registration 2026-07-28, CIMD draft cited by MCP: -00, CIMD current IETF record: -02, RFC 7591 — Dynamic Client Registration, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28.

MCP04 — Reject a substituted authorization response

Compare code interception, request confusion and issuer mix-up without treating PKCE, state and issuer checks as interchangeable.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core MCP 2026-07-28 HTTP authorization teaching profile; authorization itself is optional for MCP deployments. No deprecated session or DCR default.

Actors: Client C; Browser B; Selected authorization server A; Substitute issuer X.

Declared setup

  • A completed metadata validation and C retained issuer, verifier, redirect and state in one transaction record.
  • Primary profile advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported=true.
  • Use synthetic callbacks; the offline app never opens the supplied redirect.

Authored sequence

  1. Run an authorization request with S256, state and exact registered redirect binding.
  2. Deliver a callback to C but retain it as unaccepted input.
  3. Validate state and the response issuer against the recorded transaction; only then permit code redemption at the recorded token endpoint.
  4. A compares the verifier-derived challenge and rejects a substituted verifier or reused code.
  5. Show a separate mismatch branch ending before redemption, and a token-endpoint rejection branch ending after the request but before token issuance.
  6. Exercise the four advertised/present-iss combinations required by the pinned MCP response-validation table.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Wrong state, wrong issuer, missing advertised iss, or unexpected callback redirect.
  • Present mismatching iss even when support was not advertised: reject.
  • Both advertisement and iss absent: do not falsely claim MCP requires rejection; retain other transaction checks.
  • Mismatched issuer in an error response: do not display attacker-controlled error_description/error_uri as trusted AS output.
  • Wrong verifier, reused code or PKCE downgrade attempt.

Acceptance

  • No code is sent to an endpoint selected from the unvalidated callback.
  • Exact issuer comparison does not case-fold, remove ports or normalize trailing slashes.
  • Each failed check names the responsible actor and denied next action.
  • The PKCE fixture computes the S256 value against an independent known vector.

Primary references: RFC 9207 — Authorization response issuer, RFC 7636 — PKCE, MCP authorization 2026-07-28, RFC 9700 — OAuth security BCP, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28.

MCP05 — A received token is not yet an accepted request

Show the resource server validating a token and then authorizing one operation; contrast declared JWT and opaque-token profiles.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core HTTP resource validation with two declared implementation profiles: RFC9068 JWT or RFC7662 opaque-token introspection. Neither token format is universally required by MCP.

Actors: Client C; MCP resource R; Authorization server A.

Declared setup

  • Two explicit profiles: RFC9068 JWT access token; opaque token with authenticated RFC7662 introspection.
  • R has an issuer/audience/key or introspection configuration derived from a trusted operator profile.
  • Link to the dedicated JWT family for full JWS/JWK mechanics; do not require JWT for all MCP deployments.

Authored sequence

  1. C sends a token in the request header; show TLS receipt and application recovery as distinct moments.
  2. JWT branch parses claims without trusting them, then validates the selected token profile and intended audience.
  3. Opaque branch sends the token to the configured introspection endpoint using R credentials; receiving a JSON response is distinct from accepting active status and applicable permissions.
  4. Create an R-local validated authorization context only after the profile checks succeed.
  5. Evaluate the required scope and operation-specific resource policy against that context.
  6. Return result or the appropriate invalid-token/permission response, with client knowledge changing only on its receipt.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • ID token or token for another API supplied instead of an MCP access token.
  • Wrong issuer/audience, invalid JWT signature, expired token or opaque active=false.
  • Introspection unavailable: deny protected work under the declared fail-closed profile; do not invent active status.
  • Valid token but denied file ACL: token validation remains successful while operation is denied.

Acceptance

  • Decode, verification, scope decision and operation result have distinct state/observations.
  • JWT token bytes and decoded claims remain related representations; parsing alone creates no verified identity.
  • 401 and 403 are not conflated; introspection credentials never reach C.
  • Rejected tokens cannot cause a tool side effect or protected result disclosure.

Primary references: RFC 6750 — Bearer use, RFC 9068 — JWT access-token profile, RFC 7662 — Introspection, RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28.

MCP06 — Insufficient scope and bounded incremental consent

Explain why a valid read token cannot authorize a write, and how the client can request a deliberate upgrade.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core MCP 2026-07-28 HTTP authorization teaching profile; authorization itself is optional for MCP deployments. No deprecated session or DCR default.

Actors: Client C; User/browser B; MCP resource R; Authorization server A.

Declared setup

  • C previously requested and received files:read; new tool operation requires files:write.
  • The profile implements the current MCP scope-challenge behavior; scope names remain application-defined.
  • Authorization may be declined; no silent approval is modeled.

Authored sequence

  1. R validates the read token, then rejects the write with 403 and Bearer insufficient_scope plus operation-required scopes.
  2. C parses the challenge and shows the extra requested permission before launching a new authorization attempt.
  3. Build the reauthorization scope set from the previously requested set and current challenge; retain exact requested versus granted sets.
  4. A asks for appropriate consent and may return a smaller grant or a denial.
  5. C retries with the new token only after successful grant processing; R reevaluates the write policy.
  6. Bound retries and end with a useful permanent-error explanation when permissions still do not satisfy the operation.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Challenge scopes are not necessarily a subset of PRM scopes_supported.
  • Missing challenge scope uses the selected MCP initial-scope fallback only where applicable; do not infer unlimited access.
  • User declines, AS grants less, repeated challenge, or a broader scope hierarchy does not satisfy the local policy.
  • A scope upgrade does not override a separate per-object ACL denial.

Acceptance

  • Old token remains a historical/read-authorized object; it is not rewritten into a write token.
  • Consent denial prevents write execution without erasing unrelated accepted read state.
  • Test union calculation and retry limit independently of runtime-generated expectations.
  • Copy clearly separates 401 sign-in need from 403 additional permission.

Primary references: MCP authorization 2026-07-28, RFC 6750 — Bearer use, RFC 9728 — Protected Resource Metadata, RFC 9700 — OAuth security BCP.

MCP07 — Expiry, refresh rotation and reauthorization

Follow credential lifetime through renewal failure as well as success, with endpoint-specific knowledge.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core HTTP token-lifetime lesson; refresh issuance is discretionary. Public-client rotation is selected for this MCP baseline. RFC7009 revocation is a separately advertised optional profile.

Actors: Client C; Authorization server A; MCP resource R; User/browser B when reauthorization is needed.

Declared setup

  • Public-client profile with short-lived access token and AS-issued rotating refresh token.
  • Sibling input issues no refresh token; issuance is not guaranteed.
  • Clock, rotation and optional revocation propagation are fixed synthetic fixtures.

Authored sequence

  1. Advance time until the access token expires; local expiry prediction or an R 401 starts renewal without accepting the expired token.
  2. C sends refresh token only to A, bound to its client/resource grant; A checks validity and grant constraints.
  3. On success, A issues a new access/refresh generation and invalidates the prior refresh generation under the selected rotation policy.
  4. C acquires the replacement before updating its current credential store; replay exposes old/new exact IDs and retention separately.
  5. On invalid_grant, missing refresh token or revocation, discard unusable current credentials and offer a new authorization-code flow.
  6. Optional advertised RFC7009 branch separates C revocation request, A invalidation and R knowledge/propagation; disconnect alone does not imply token revocation.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Reuse of a rotated refresh token; attempted scope/resource escalation through refresh.
  • Refresh rejection or transient network failure must not cause unbounded loops.
  • offline_access is not an MCP resource permission and cannot be assumed supported or sufficient to obtain refresh.
  • A revoked self-contained token may not be known immediately to an offline validator; expose the declared enforcement policy.

Acceptance

  • Refresh token never appears at R, in a URL, or in exported diagnostic text.
  • Old token possession, AS invalidation and R rejection are distinct facts.
  • Public-client rotation is shown for this MCP profile; generic OAuth alternatives are not silently substituted.
  • Expiry and renewal are repeatable under a deterministic clock.

Primary references: MCP authorization 2026-07-28, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28, RFC 9700 — OAuth security BCP, RFC 7009 — Token revocation, RFC 6750 — Bearer use.

MCP08 — OAuth permission, tool approval and resource policy

Distinguish identity evidence, a transport access grant, a host decision to invoke a tool, and the server decision for the target object.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core per-request HTTP authorization plus separately declared host approval and resource ACL policies; the host UI is not a protocol grant.

Actors: User U; Host and MCP client C; MCP resource R; Resource policy evaluator P.

Declared setup

  • C already holds a valid scoped token; no new login is needed.
  • The lab host requires explicit approval for its synthetic destructive tool.
  • The server has a separate per-object policy; this approval UI is a declared host policy, not a new OAuth grant.

Authored sequence

  1. List tools under the authorization supplied on that request; show that a listed capability is not a promised successful mutation.
  2. The model proposes a tool call; C displays concrete tool/target/arguments for the host approval decision.
  3. If U declines, C sends no tools/call and retains the OAuth token unchanged.
  4. If U approves, C sends a fresh authenticated POST; R validates its authorization and P checks the chosen target.
  5. Return either a policy denial with no side effect or a completed operation result.
  6. Contrast AS sign-in/consent with this host approval and server authorization on separate cards.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Valid grant plus user denial; user approval plus ACL denial; untrusted tool annotations pretending an operation is harmless.
  • Changed arguments after approval invalidate the declared host approval record.
  • Self-asserted MCP clientInfo/capabilities cannot substitute for authentication.
  • Cached tool list from another authorization context must not bypass the current request decision.

Acceptance

  • Expose independent booleans for tokenAccepted, hostInvocationApproved, resourceAuthorized and operationExecuted.
  • Denied invocation creates no fictitious network exchange.
  • No OIDC ID token or universal subject claim is invented merely because OAuth is used.
  • Keyboard users can inspect the concrete operation and decline without losing journey focus.

Primary references: MCP tools 2026-07-28, MCP authorization 2026-07-28, RFC 9068 — JWT access-token profile, RFC 9700 — OAuth security BCP.

MCP09 — MCP proxy: a separate OAuth grant for the upstream API

Show both trust boundaries and the two different access tokens when an MCP server calls another protected service.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Optional deployment topology using core HTTP authorization on the MCP boundary and an independent upstream OAuth grant; not mandatory for every server.

Actors: Client C; User/browser B; MCP proxy P; MCP authorization server A; Upstream authorization server UAS; Upstream API U.

Declared setup

  • C-to-P authorization already uses a token with P as resource.
  • P is separately registered as an OAuth client at UAS; no upstream token is initially available.
  • Use two collapsed chapters so only one authorization boundary is expanded at a time.

Authored sequence

  1. P accepts C authorization for the requested MCP operation, then discovers that upstream access is absent.
  2. P binds an upstream authorization transaction to the initiating user/client/operation and obtains the required consent.
  3. B authorizes at UAS; P redeems that upstream code using its own registered client configuration.
  4. P stores the separately issued upstream token with its own audience, issuer and grant record.
  5. P calls U with that token; U independently validates and authorizes the requested API operation.
  6. P accepts the upstream result and returns the permitted MCP result to C without exposing upstream credentials.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Upstream consent denied; upstream token expired; U rejects its audience or ACL.
  • The C token cannot fill the missing upstream-token slot.
  • One user/client grant must not be reused as another user/client grant.
  • If a product instead uses token exchange, it requires a separately sourced extension profile; do not silently claim it happened here.

Acceptance

  • Two exact token IDs, two intended resources and two authorization contexts remain visible.
  • P receiving the U response is distinct from interpreting its accepted result.
  • Failure of the upstream hop does not retroactively invalidate the accepted C-to-P token.
  • No password/code/token is collected by ordinary tool arguments or leaked into tool output.

Primary references: MCP authorization security 2026-07-28, MCP security best practices 2026-07-28, RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators, RFC 7636 — PKCE, RFC 6750 — Bearer use.

MCP10 — Proxy consent cannot be inherited by a different MCP client

Demonstrate the confused-deputy boundary with an existing upstream login/consent cookie and a newly introduced downstream client.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Optional proxy topology with required consent isolation for the depicted clients. Historical DCR attack context is deprecated compatibility, not a recommended onboarding default.

Actors: User/browser B; Previously approved client C1; New client C2; MCP proxy P; Upstream authorization server UAS.

Declared setup

  • P uses one registered upstream client ID; B already has an upstream consent cookie.
  • C1 is approved for this user; C2 is not.
  • The historically documented attack can use DCR; the core lesson is consent isolation, not a recommendation to deploy deprecated registration.

Authored sequence

  1. Show the prior C1 approval record and upstream browser cookie as separate artifacts.
  2. C2 requests proxy access with its own registered redirect and requested upstream permission set.
  3. P checks the user/client-specific consent record before starting the upstream authorization attempt.
  4. P presents C2 identity, target redirect hostname and requested upstream access; refusal ends the attempt.
  5. Only explicit approval creates the C2 consent record; any upstream automatic sign-in/consent behavior cannot create that record on its own.
  6. Bind callback/state and the resulting grant to the approved C2 transaction.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • A global user-has-consented flag, C1 cookie replay, mismatched redirect, CSRF token mismatch or tampered consent record.
  • A display name resembling C1 is not an identity match.
  • An upstream consent cookie must not produce a downstream code for an unapproved client.

Acceptance

  • The default safe path blocks before contacting UAS when consent is absent/denied.
  • No real malicious redirect is opened; the attack input is a frozen synthetic fixture.
  • Tests assert zero downstream authorization/code release before matching consent.
  • Explain exactly which approval must be renewed, avoiding a generic login failed message.

Primary references: MCP security best practices 2026-07-28, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28, MCP client registration 2026-07-28, RFC 9700 — OAuth security BCP.

MCP11 — Reject token passthrough across the proxy boundary

Make wrong-recipient token acceptance and downstream forwarding visibly separate forbidden transitions.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core MCP 2026-07-28 HTTP authorization teaching profile; authorization itself is optional for MCP deployments. No deprecated session or DCR default.

Actors: Client C; MCP proxy P; Upstream API U; Their respective authorization servers.

Declared setup

  • A synthetic upstream token is valid for U but not P.
  • A separate valid P token and separately issued U token are available for the corrected comparison.
  • No permissive broken path is presented as a selectable production configuration.

Authored sequence

  1. C presents the U token to P as if it authorized MCP access.
  2. P receives and inspects the token, rejects the intended-recipient check and returns an invalid-token response.
  3. The blocked route to U remains visibly inactive; there is no token forwarding or upstream side effect.
  4. Switch to the corrected comparison: P accepts its own resource token.
  5. P obtains/selects the separate U token under MCP09 and uses only that token for U.
  6. Display the two validation records and the rejected token history without promoting rejected possession to authority.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • JWT with wrong aud, opaque token whose authoritative metadata identifies U, or a token from an unrelated issuer.
  • Valid P token forwarded unchanged to U is also disallowed.
  • No fallback forwards an unrecognized token merely because P cannot parse it.

Acceptance

  • Assert U receives no request in the rejected attempt.
  • Incoming/outgoing token object identities differ in the successful proxy path.
  • A user-readable token error does not echo secret token bytes.
  • Audience rejection remains correct with matching scope names at P and U.

Primary references: MCP authorization security 2026-07-28, RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators, RFC 9068 — JWT access-token profile, RFC 7662 — Introspection.

MCP12 — Untrusted discovery URLs and metadata do not trigger unsafe fetches

Teach metadata and authorization-URL validation with an offline simulation of redirects, DNS results and credential destinations.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core authorization security demonstrated with fixed offline fixtures; deployment-specific network allowlists are explicit local policy.

Actors: Client C or metadata-fetching AS; Synthetic metadata source M; Synthetic policy/egress gate G.

Declared setup

  • Fixed input fixtures include a legitimate public URL, private/link-local targets, redirect chains and changed DNS answers.
  • The shipping learning app performs no actual discovery/token/authorization fetch from user-provided values.
  • Enterprise private-network exceptions, if shown, are explicit administrator allowlists rather than universal unsafe exceptions.

Authored sequence

  1. Receive a metadata/authorization/CIMD URL as untrusted input.
  2. Validate scheme, authority and deployment policy before any simulated request; separately evaluate each redirected/resolved destination.
  3. Model bounded response size/time, trusted TLS identity and metadata schema/resource/issuer checks.
  4. At a denied destination, stop before a simulated credential-bearing POST or browser navigation.
  5. Show that accepted metadata still grants no user access and cannot transfer an existing issuer credential to a new issuer.
  6. Render the reason and a redacted diagnostic event; retain no real URL query secret.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • javascript/data/file authorization URL; HTTPS URL redirecting to loopback/link-local; DNS rebinding; invalid TLS identity.
  • Poisoned token_endpoint; resource_metadata naming a different resource; CIMD mismatch.
  • A same-hostname but different issuer path attempts credential reuse.
  • Oversized or cyclic metadata/redirect chain exhausts a bounded budget.

Acceptance

  • Network interception tests observe zero external application requests in source HTTP, standalone HTTP and file modes.
  • Assertions distinguish blocked-before-send from rejected-after-response.
  • Document model policy versus normative requirements; a private enterprise AS is not universally forbidden by MCP.
  • Source links are explicit user navigation, never automatic page-load fetches or OAuth launches.

Primary references: RFC 9728 — Protected Resource Metadata, RFC 8414 — Authorization Server Metadata, MCP authorization security 2026-07-28, MCP security best practices 2026-07-28, CIMD draft cited by MCP: -00.

MCP13 — Local stdio: process credentials and OS authority

Explain why local subprocess access follows process/credential boundaries rather than the remote HTTP OAuth challenge.

Delivery: core. Protocol/deployment scope: Core stdio transport, outside the MCP HTTP OAuth authorization mechanism. Environment/secret-provider and OS policy are declared local deployment behavior.

Actors: Host C; Local MCP subprocess S; OS credential store / launcher O; Optional upstream API U.

Declared setup

  • MCP 2026-07-28 stdio transport; a restricted synthetic process profile.
  • S receives only its configured credential via its declared launcher/secret-provider path.
  • No real subprocess, OS secret or network access is performed by the simulator.

Authored sequence

  1. C launches the modeled subprocess under the selected OS identity and restricted environment.
  2. O supplies the per-server credential; label the provider action and resulting local possession.
  3. C and S exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout; do not insert an HTTP 401/WWW-Authenticate flow.
  4. S attempts a local resource action under OS policy or uses its separately obtained upstream credential.
  5. An OS/resource policy decision determines the operation result; MCP transport alone does not sandbox S.
  6. On termination show the modeled credential cleanup separately from upstream token validity/revocation.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Missing environment/secret-provider value; OS file denial; missing upstream scope.
  • A global inherited credential would be overbroad; use a visible bad-configuration fixture, not the default.
  • HTTP-to-stdio proxy would introduce a remote boundary requiring its own declared protection.
  • MCP roots or tool approval are not an OS containment guarantee.

Acceptance

  • No browser authorization grant appears unless a separately selected upstream library actually uses one.
  • Local identity, token authority and allowed file access stay independent.
  • Cross-link workstation/PAM/LSM material instead of inventing platform behavior here.
  • Diagnostics never print environment values or inherited real file paths.

Primary references: MCP stdio 2026-07-28, MCP local server security 2026-07-28, MCP authorization 2026-07-28.

MCP14 — Optional machine client: client-credentials extension

Show an application obtaining its own authorization without pretending to be an interactively authenticated user.

Delivery: optional. Protocol/deployment scope: Optional io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials extension, explicitly enabled and version/snapshot-pinned; not a core mandatory user authorization flow.

Actors: Confidential machine client C; Authorization server A; MCP resource R.

Declared setup

  • Explicitly enabled io.modelcontextprotocol/oauth-client-credentials extension and compatible client/server policy.
  • Pre-registered confidential client; choose private_key_jwt authentication or a secret-based comparison.
  • Current extension source must be pinned by snapshot/hash at implementation freeze; no made-up extension version.

Authored sequence

  1. C declares extension support through the current per-request capabilities profile.
  2. C creates a short-lived signed client assertion, or selects its securely configured secret-based authentication method.
  3. C requests grant_type=client_credentials with the intended resource and application scopes at A.
  4. A validates client authentication and application policy, then issues an access token for R.
  5. C sends a version-correct authenticated POST; R validates the token and authorizes the machine operation.
  6. At expiry, C obtains another client-credentials token; do not fabricate a browser or assume refresh_token grant support.

Named negative and compatibility inputs

  • Extension unsupported or policy disallows machine access.
  • Bad assertion signature/audience/expiry, reused jti under the selected replay-protection profile, or invalid secret.
  • Valid client authentication but requested application scope denied.
  • Machine token must not inherit a human subject or an existing user consent record.

Acceptance

  • JWT assertion, private key and resulting access token have separate identities and holder permissions.
  • Private signing key never leaves C; assertion is delivered to A, not used as R bearer token.
  • No mandatory-core label, interactive consent event or guaranteed refresh token.
  • Cross-link JWT client-assertion validation; do not mislabel client authentication as JWT bearer authorization grant.

Primary references: Optional OAuth client-credentials extension, RFC 6749 — Client credentials, RFC 7523 — Client assertion, RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators, RFC 6750 — Bearer use.

Do not generate expected behavior from runtime output.
  • Unit/model checks must cover the issuer table, metadata path ordering, registration selection, per-issuer isolation, PKCE verifier comparison, resource/scope distinctions, token replacement, no-passthrough, consent isolation and bounded retries. Reuse independent JWT/PKCE numeric fixtures where applicable; mark modeled/fixture evidence separately from live interoperability.
  • Mounted UI checks: choose every lesson by ID/title/search/route; inspect real operational fields; activate Replay path and exact replay; compare before/at/after validation or denial and canonical full-prefix equality. Check focus after scope upgrades, registration failure, cancellation and journey replacement.
  • Current artifact native evidence: all 13 required starters, MCP14 if included, plus representative metadata mismatch, rejected callback, denied scope, refresh failure, proxy denial and stdio/extension paths in source HTTP, standalone HTTP and standalone file. Add desktop/mobile captures that actually show metadata choice, rejected issuer, scoped upgrade, two token audiences and local stdio contrast; do not misname a final unrelated inspector as replay evidence.
  • Test keyboard-only navigation, visible focus destination, narrow viewport scrolling, complete exact inventory and long metadata/issuer strings. Preserve protocol state across tabs and display toggles. No product-wide native or real-AT claims from a bounded sample; G01 and inherited performance gaps retain their current dispositions.
  • Record exact source/runner/fixture/build hashes, source snapshots or immutable revision links for mutable extension/draft material, browser/runtime versions, failed attempts and final reports. Offline network assertions must remain zero-outbound for every loading mode; manual primary-source link opening is distinct.
  • Before implementation freeze recheck the dated MCP pages and IETF draft status. If a conflict affects modeled behavior, record a source-discrepancy note and resolve the profile explicitly; do not silently cherry-pick tutorial, 2025 sessions, 2026 metadata and newer drafts into one supposedly normative flow.

Two deeper RFC Editor requests later returned HTTP 429; RFC 9728 was also read from the IETF copy, and the response-issuer rules are directly stated by the dated MCP specification. No extension release tag was asserted where the public extension page supplies none; source snapshot/hash pinning is an implementation gate.

Integration, performance, usability and acceptance

Build on the accepted corrections2/source snapshot and standalone SHA-256 9a3fc759c77502b52dd7b4d5da0851d706b36e7a0bf0afbe73aca0555798e924. Preserve the accepted Windows, Network, PAKE, Kerberos and SMB repairs. This remains an offline teaching application with authored protocol fixtures, not a live authentication client, credential collector or production authorization service. Keep protocol modeling, independently verified numeric examples and actual platform interoperability as separate claims.

Phase 0 — safe follow-up and a measured performance foundation

  1. Make the narrow WIN-11 repair. In src/windows-auth-lab.js, author the host-local creation of the acceptor subkey in the field-operation ledger for the raw CredSSP AP-REP path. Keep the same artifact, creator/holder, plain representation, source event and exact-value reference. The affected scope is the six fixed W09/W11/W13/W14/W15/W16 presets and their seven named variants listed in corrections2/windows-recheck.txt. Their exact held-object histories and client acceptance boundaries are already correct. Never add the plain subkey to wire objects to make it visible to field replay; never duplicate the existing held-object creation. A host-local operation before the AP-REP send, or a separately authored local preparation event, is acceptable when its projection and carrier boundaries remain consistent.
  2. Verify that repair narrowly. One focused regression across the affected builder paths must show host creation → client validated installation in field replay, unchanged exact-object history, no plaintext key send/receive, and no early client possession. Include an unaffected local-preparation path as the control. Use the existing attribute/held-object replay APIs, not a new fixture-only substitute. Rebuild and check the affected emitted journey when the authoring shape changes. Do not rerun the complete legacy browser matrix or full suite solely for this minor presentation fix.
  3. Measure the accepted build before selecting an optimization. Retain the accepted source/HTML as an immutable comparison input. On the same machine/browser/runtime, measure accepted → optimized foundation and, later, optimized foundation → complete expansion. Record cold readiness, human-query picker filtering, selection, replay start and search during active playback in source HTTP, standalone HTTP and standalone file:. Use equivalent queries and actual UI actions in both versions, alternate fresh contexts, retain every sample and document warm-up/cache conditions. A small sample is descriptive, not statistically conclusive.
  4. Preserve the existing material threshold. A flag requires both a median increase above 25% and above 100 ms for startup, or above 25% and above 50 ms for an interaction. Preserve flagged raw observations and investigate them; do not adjust the threshold to make an optimization pass. The seven historical flags belong to predecessor artifact 92ab1782…; a new accepted-build baseline neither remeasures nor silently clears that older comparison.
  5. Optimize the measured cost, then proceed with catalog growth. Existing historical traces implicate the larger visible field index's paint/prepaint/layout work and picker/catalog layout. Reconfirm on the accepted current build with the permanent tools/verification/profile-expansion-replay.mjs approach, including the real index-open/index-closed control. Raw CPU profiles and Chrome traces are attribution evidence; do not substitute their instrumented times for uninstrumented acceptance medians or sum overlapping inclusive trace durations.

Concrete investigation points are AuthFlowStudio.renderAttributeIndex(), indexContext() and renderCatalog() in src/app.js, plus filterScenarioOptions() and ScenarioPicker.render() in src/scenario-picker.js. The current index sorts and constructs field rows, resolves scenario contexts and usage counts; keyed row reuse already avoids some replacement. The picker normalizes option text while filtering and rebuilds grouped results. Start with reusable sorted static metadata, pre-normalized search text, indexed membership and revision-keyed usage/context data, then measure whether DOM/paint work still dominates. These are hypotheses, not a prescribed optimization outcome.

Cache immutable catalog data separately from context-dependent definitions and canonical step usage. Key scenario/configuration caches by their real context/revision, normalized configuration and relevant authenticator/profile; invalidate on Apply, Reset, route/profile change and model replacement. Do not cache rendered identity/realm/issuer values across environments. Do not regenerate every model merely to display step counts. No global index rebuild belongs in the animation-frame loop. Any DOM reduction, containment, incremental rendering or windowing must preserve logical result order, selected-row identity, keyboard reachability, active-descendant validity and screen-reader availability. Do not declare success by silently closing the default field pane, removing global discovery, skipping results or changing the benchmark question. Retain the existing journey-scoped initial index for profiled lessons and global typed search.

Navigation and cross-group journeys

Extend metadata-driven navigation rather than adding another row of tiny tabs. Use a grouped, searchable workspace selector with a clearly announced current workspace/family, a compact starter surface and full catalog search. Keep the same capabilities reachable on desktop, narrow layouts and keyboard. Preserve all existing canonical hashes, scenario IDs and aliases; unsupported routes must continue to take the documented fallback without leaking transaction values into URLs.

WorkstationsNew routed workspace; Windows sign-in/elevation, Linux sign-in/elevation and macOS sign-in/elevation families. Each opens a curated beginner journey.Local logon identity, network credentials, session creation and privilege/authorization decisions are separate. PAM identity/authentication processing and LSM enforcement are not one actor or one acceptance result.

Use relatedLessons and the existing renderLearningProfile() related-journey controls for three explicit learning paths: (1) nonjoined local workstation sign-in → explicit domain credentials → the accepted SMB access journey; (2) local/Linux/macOS session → the selected NFS authentication/identity-mapping profile → file access decision; (3) JWT validation → Kubernetes authentication and RBAC, or the appropriate MCP protected-resource flow. Label what carries conceptually into the next lesson and what new credentials, trust or configuration it assumes. Following a link starts the destination's authored context; it must not imply that browser navigation transferred a real ticket, token, logon session or elevated privilege.

If a genuinely continuous demonstration is needed, author one composite canonical model with namespaced event/object IDs and explicit handoff events, mappings and credential lineage. Do not concatenate step arrays blindly or pass hidden mutable authentication state between independent lessons. A local account may access a domain resource using separately supplied credentials without changing its local desktop identity; the path must explain that distinction before Play. An NFS branch must use its own stated security flavor and identity-mapping assumptions rather than inheriting SMB's result. In an AUTH_SYS lesson, label UID/GID information as client-asserted; TLS channel authentication must not silently turn that assertion into cryptographically authenticated per-user identity.

Create a new versioned planning/evidence area, for example docs/next-expansion/ and docs/verification/next-expansion/. Preserve predecessor reports without relabeling them. Mark a standards-only or uncertain profile explicitly; never convert uncertainty into an invented universal behavior. Retain small relevant snapshots/fixture inputs with hashes where appropriate and give regeneration instructions.
  • Message and operation ledger: sender/receiver, exact representation, protection/key/context lineage, carried versus locally computed fields, receiver-local decode/check and canonical event/milestone. Distinguish network transfer, local IPC, local computation and an exchange folded onto one physical card. PAM, LSASS and LSM processing must use their actual local subsystem boundaries; never invent network packets to connect local checks, and do not turn genuine local IPC between different owners into a self-operation. Merely listing a field in prose or payload cannot establish its ownership or replay.
  • Object/holding ledger: separate artifact, representation and holding IDs; creator, exact value/reference, logical owner/store, permitted readers, acquire/use/release/replace events, derived-from identity and retained authority state. A ciphertext receipt grants only the wire holding until the authored decrypt/check event. Visibility, decoding, trust and acceptance are distinct: a signed JWT payload is readable before signature/claim validation and must be displayed as untrusted, not falsely hidden as ciphertext. Decoding alone never installs a trusted identity. Grant readable or accepted state only at the appropriate authored event for that representation; do not confuse the two grants. A failed check does not erase prior credential disclosure, credentials already cached, or the evidence that a message was received.
  • Outcome ledger: independently state server acceptance, client knowledge, session creation, authorization decision, protected-result receipt and result verification. For denials, say who knows what and when. A JWT signature, PAM authentication result, UAC/sudo authorization step, Kubernetes role match or NFS credential mapping must not automatically imply every later access decision.
  • Replay invariants: full journey, connection, field and exact-object replay must reconstruct the same complete canonical prefix at the same cursor. At least one meaningful local operation and one protected receipt/acceptance boundary per family need actual mounted replay checks. Verify exact value and representation, not merely a label or number of trace rows. Check reset, seek backward, replay exit and scenario/context change for stale secrets, holdings or selected objects.
  • Evidence identity: record exact source/manifest/worksheet hashes, runner hash, argv, exit status, runtime/browser/dependency versions, standalone hash/bytes, before/after identity, raw logs, screenshot hashes and findings. Keep failed/superseded runs with their status. Missing tools or incomplete scope produce an explicit unverified/partial result, never synthetic success. Reuse unchanged historical evidence only under its own identity and clearly bounded claim.

For numeric cryptographic claims, extend the isolated tools/verification/expansion-crypto/ verifier or a similarly isolated next-phase QA package. Pin dependencies and runtime, retain official vectors or independently generated deterministic fixtures and their provenance, and compare with an oracle independent of the application builder. Negative cases need documented mutated input and expected rejection, including wrong context/recipient/key where the profile requires it. Printing a fixture, recomputing an expected value with the same helper or passing a UI assertion is not numerical verification. Keep SYM(...)/HANDLE(...) material explicit whenever the lesson does not model real encoded bytes. No QA package becomes a runtime app dependency, no CDN/import/browser download is added to the application, and a numeric pass never becomes a live-platform interoperability claim.

Teaching and accessibility acceptance

  • Before Play, display the concrete question, profile/platform version, starting identities/credentials/trust and precise completion boundary through the existing learning-profile panel. Start each family with a small curated successful journey and a discoverable meaningful denial/comparison; keep advanced protocol switches out of the beginner entry flow.
  • Default to the useful physical topology; expand local actors on demand. Preserve independent PAM conversation, identity lookup, authorization/session decisions and LSM policy enforcement where the selected Linux profile models them. Explain similar Windows/macOS concepts through their own sourced subsystem roles rather than renaming them PAM. Privilege, principal, credential store and session are separate inspector facts.
  • Global search must find protocols, user questions, abbreviations, platform/profile names and relevant fields. Filtering must not activate another scenario, pause/reset playback or steal focus. Selecting a result deliberately changes context. Preserve caret/composition and platform text-editing shortcuts; maintain a valid combobox active descendant, result announcement and visible keyboard focus.
  • Keep field names and concise values readable by default; long JWTs, claims, security descriptors and key material expand in the inspector. Do not squeeze the actor graph to illegibility at narrow widths. Use the existing intentional graph-scroll/external-inventory mode and ensure sticky controls do not cover focused targets.
  • Test Tab/Shift+Tab, arrows/Home/End where applicable, Enter, Escape and F2 through workspace/family/search, graph, exact inventory, related journeys and source links. Nested help must restore the exact initiating control when it still exists. Search/index optimization must not substitute another object generation or focus a hidden legacy select.
  • Source links must have meaningful standard/section labels, be keyboard reachable, preserve safe new-tab behavior and visibly indicate external documentation. Use target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" as the current renderer does. Opening documentation is user-initiated navigation that may need connectivity; the lesson, source metadata and replay remain useful offline. Do not fetch specifications, discovery documents, JWKS or remote assets at application runtime.
  • Validate native desktop/narrow geometry, folded/expanded internals, local-operation paths, inventory overflow, long configured identifiers, reduced motion, actual touch interactions and actual browser-menu 200%/400% zoom. CSS viewport simulations are useful separate checks and must not be relabeled as real zoom. Use representative cases from every new family and dense/problematic combinations, not a screenshot of one successful default.

G01 remains a release condition. A human must exercise the actual app with a named screen reader/browser/OS combination and record whether the scenario, current step, logical owner/holding, local versus network operation, validation result and focus return are understandable. Include search, nested help, replay/seek and at least one denial. Automated ARIA/DOM checks and screenshots do not close this gate. The worker should complete authorized implementation and produce a review candidate while an unavailable manual check is explicitly open; do not add repeated permission requests or call the candidate fully release-ready before the required manual evidence exists.

Bounded delivery sequence

DeliveryScope and evidence before moving on
P0. Preserve and improve the foundationWIN-11 safe fix; fresh accepted-build measurements; attributable index/picker optimization; focused replay/focus/search-during-playback checks; before/after native timing and raw profiles. Freeze the optimized baseline for expansion comparison. Do not begin mass catalog addition while the measured growth bottleneck is unexplained.
P0–P1. Shared contract and navigationSource/profile matrices, manifests, collision checks and the new grouped navigation/routes. Integrate one representative authored lesson and holding builder per new workspace as a vertical slice before multiplying cases. Verify old links and the Files→SMB shortcut, keyboard navigation and emitted module registration. Mark partial families as partial.
P1–P2. File and workstation journeysImplement the committed Windows/Linux/macOS sign-in/elevation and NFS worksheet branches in bounded family slices. Reuse accepted SMB through explicit related navigation. Each slice gets its relevant source/held/replay/negative tests and targeted native coverage for changed boundaries; no automatic full historical sweep after every wording fix.
P3–P5. JWT, Kubernetes and MCPComplete JWT foundations first so later lessons reference a consistent verification vocabulary. Implement dedicated Kubernetes identity and authorization families, then MCP profiles, using their own sources/actors/acceptance boundaries. Add cross-group learning links and independent numeric QA where numeric claims are made. Do not wait until packaging to author failure predicates or exact-object histories.
P6. Integrate and finalize onceOn the frozen final candidate run the full source suite, universal held-object coverage and compiled smoke over every deduplicated choice. Exercise all new/changed scenario semantics in the three native loading modes, with representative legacy smoke and risk-driven additional checks for changed shared code. Complete the new-family geometry/keyboard/touch/actual-zoom matrix and final comparative performance run. Record manual G01 separately. Reopen broad checks only when a concrete later change invalidates their evidence.

Keep expensive browser/performance work separate from the bounded full regression generator to avoid measurement contention. Preserve the current run-regressions.mjs inventory discovery and bounded concurrency; tests should assert meaningful independently authored boundaries, not incidental wording. Add tests/<family>.test.mjs, tests/held-object-<family>.test.mjs and targeted mounted replay/navigation checks as warranted. Reuse held-objects-check.mjs, compiled-bundle-smoke.mjs and actual native runner infrastructure; extend coverage from the agreed manifest instead of copying historical numeric constants. A shared renderer, route or state-engine change may justify broader affected coverage; a local minor copy/projection fix alone does not.

Final worker handoff checklist

  • Complete source, reproducible offline build and exact final standalone; a concise change summary and per-family manifest showing implemented, partial, unsupported and deferred items with explicit reasons. No silent omissions or invented fixed totals.
  • Versioned primary-source/profile matrix, independent protocol/ownership/outcome worksheets, precise support assumptions and known ambiguities. Default lessons follow the selected current supported profiles; legacy comparisons appear only when their authentication differences teach a requested distinction.
  • Fresh final source/test/manifest/runner/artifact identities, full-suite raw logs, all-choice compiled and held-object coverage, targeted three-mode native results, screenshot identities, actual keyboard/touch/zoom records, numeric QA evidence and current performance comparisons. Clearly separate automated/native/manual/live-interoperability evidence.
  • Retained failures and historical results; explicit open G01 and any remaining material performance flags or platform uncertainties. Address actionable regressions or carry their concrete release disposition; do not hide them inside a top-level passed:true.
  • One clearly named worker/reviewer handoff document, standalone HTML, source archive and verification archive. If captures are split into an overlay, document extraction and verify every referenced path/hash across the delivered pair. Generate package status/checksums and include them in the handoff; rebuild an extracted source package and compare it byte-for-byte with the delivered HTML.

This plan does not require another logo iteration, remote assets, telemetry, live endpoint calls or a broader deployment task. Preserve the existing CSP policy and supplied icons. Finish each authorized phase with concrete evidence and report the remaining phase scope; do not turn internal quality gates into repeated approval interruptions.

Final delivery and review contract

Keep the worker handoff unambiguous. At each phase, use one phase-labelled artifact stem and identify its source and standalone hashes in one handoff document. The submitted set is the standalone application, buildable source archive and verification archive; the handoff points to exact evidence records. Include package status and SHA256SUMS in the verification archive instead of leaving them only in an external packaging directory.

  1. Report plan ID → runtime ID → implemented profile → source sections → contract/tests → current evidence. Classify each row as implemented, partial, unsupported or optional/deferred. Preserve names and reasons; all core rows must be implemented before claiming plan completion.
  2. Include the full new-family fixtures, source/profile ledger, exact synthetic manifests/configurations, build instructions, independent worksheets and raw verification logs. Copying narrative into a profile card is not completion of its event sequence.
  3. Rebuild the extracted source archive and compare the emitted standalone byte-for-byte. Resolve every current evidence path/hash across the source and any documented overlay. Keep failed and predecessor evidence labeled and separate.
  4. Provide readable results for source tests, all-choice compiled smoke, held-object coverage, current three-mode native checks, performance and any numeric vectors. State which results were actually executed. Automated, manual and live-platform results remain separate.
  5. Preserve closed findings and all 214 baseline choices. Retain open G01, unresolved material performance issues and platform/source discrepancies explicitly; a top-level passed flag must not hide them.

Beginner-flow acceptance: the first viewport should expose the learning question, key starting identities, Play and the beginning of the useful flow. Put long source ledgers, platform caveats and cryptographic internals in accessible expandable details. Preserve their discoverability without making every new lesson start with several screens of prose.

Scope boundary: logo redesign, live credential handling, external authentication calls, deployment and new unrelated protocol families are not part of this plan. Optional extensions are separately labeled. Research snapshots and platform validation still need to be captured by the worker where the detailed ledger says pending; the planning research is not a claim that those immutable bytes or live test machines were supplied.

This document was checked for unique scenario IDs, core/optional counts, required scenario fields, internal links, accepted-baseline identity and existing-scenario cross-links. It contains implementation requirements and researched sources, not a report that the new features already pass tests.

      "id": "NFS11",
      "slug": "lab-nfs-tls-auth-sys",
      "phase": "must-build core",
      "title": "RPC-with-TLS protects a transport, not a user claim",
      "goal": "Explain server-only versus mutual host authentication while preserving AUTH_SYS’s identity limits.",
      "profile": "NFS-LINUX-R1: offline Linux-oriented standards illustration, revision2026-10-21. TCP; supported optional features explicitly fixed; no tested kernel/build claim. NFSv4.2/TCP; sec=sys; default xprtsec=mtls, named tls comparison; TLS1.3 RFC9846; TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, X25519, ECDSA P-256 certificate signatures (ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256), no resumption/0-RTT.",
      "actors": [
        "Local users on one client",
        "Client RPC/TLS endpoint",
        "Server RPC/TLS endpoint and export policy",
        "Local certificate/trust stores"
      ],
      "preconditions": [
        "TLS helper configured, explicit trust and host authorization policy.",
        "Visible server/client certificate identities; different endpoint private-key handles.",
        "Apply the ALPN discrepancy disposition in the source notes before coding the wire flight."
      ],
      "steps": [
        "Use the RPC NULL procedure with empty AUTH_TLS credential and empty AUTH_NONE verifier. Accept only MSG_ACCEPTED with an AUTH_NONE verifier containing the eight ASCII octets STARTTLS; then start TLS on that same TCP connection. The probe accept_stat is not itself the TLS-support criterion.",
        "Perform TLS1.3, including the server request for a client identity; tls may accept no client certificate, mtls requires the selected valid identity.",
        "Separate certificate receipt, local handshake-key derivation/decryption, certificate/proof validation and established transport.",
        "Carry AUTH_SYS RPC in application-data ciphertext, followed by receiver-local decoded RPC.",
        "Show two client user IDs on the same host transport; apply export/squash/file policy independently for each."
      ],
      "negativeCases": [
        "Client certificate absent in required-mtls profile: transport not admitted.",
        "Valid client certificate but host unauthorized: no accepted association.",
        "Valid TLS with forged UID: no invented user-identity proof.",
        "Corrupted application-data record: no decoded RPC or file effect."
      ],
      "acceptance": [
        "Only outer TLS record is visible on wire; decoded RPC appears at the receiver’s actual decrypt event.",
        "No HTTPS wrapping or separate invented NFS-TLS port.",
        "Each endpoint derives its own directional traffic-secret objects; private keys never move.",
        "TLS-only and mTLS badges describe hosts; sec=sys remains client-asserted user identity."

    {
      "id": "WLOG01",
      "title": "Workgroup workstation: local password logon",
      "goal": "Follow a local account from credential collection through SAM validation, interactive-logon authorization and a usable desktop; show where an access token first exists.",
      "tier": "core",
      "actors": [
        "U: user",
        "L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider",
        "A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role",
        "P: user process/session and kernel token role",
        "S: local SAM authority"
      ],
      "preconditions": [
        "Windows11 supported Enterprise/Pro reference; workgroup PC WORKGROUPPC; LOCAL bob is a standard user.",
        "Password provider; no domain, cloud account, Hello or automatic sign-in; local policy permits console logon."
      ],
      "steps": [
        {
          "id": "collect",
          "from": "U",
          "to": "L",
          "type": "local-input",
          "action": "Select WORKGROUPPC\\bob and enter the synthetic password. Credential collection is not authentication.",
          "artifacts": [
            "account-scope",
            "credential-input-buffer"
          ],
          "boundary": "No authenticated identity or token yet."
        },
        {
          "id": "submit",
          "from": "L",
          "to": "A",
          "type": "local-call",
          "action": "Submit the declared interactive-logon request and selected authentication package.",
          "artifacts": [
            "interactive-logon-request"
          ],
          "boundary": "Local IPC, never an HTTP/NTLM challenge exchange."
        },
        {
          "id": "verify",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "S",
          "type": "local-call",
          "action": "The local package validates the submitted credential against the SAM account authority and returns account/group data.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-account-verifier",
            "validation-result"
          ],
          "boundary": "Only S/A learn verification success at their actual boundaries."
        },
        {
          "id": "authorize",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "A",
          "type": "local-check",
          "action": "Evaluate console logon rights and account restrictions, then form the new logon session and primary token.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-logon-policy",
            "logon-LUID",
            "primary-token"
          ],
          "boundary": "Authentication alone does not bypass an explicit deny right."
        },
        {
          "id": "desktop",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "local-create",
          "action": "Attach the token to userinit/shell startup, load the selected profile, then mark desktop ready.",
          "artifacts": [
            "primary-token",
            "profile",
            "desktop-session"
          ],
          "boundary": "Token availability precedes successful profile/desktop startup."
        },
        {
          "id": "access",
          "from": "P",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "local-check",
          "action": "Evaluate one declared file DACL with this token; record grant separately from sign-in.",
          "artifacts": [
            "file-security-descriptor",
            "access-decision"
          ],
          "boundary": "A signed-in user can still be denied a file."
        }
      ],
      "negativeCases": [
        {
          "id": "bad-password",
          "detector": "S",
          "condition": "Local verifier mismatch",
          "stopBoundary": "verify",
          "preserved": "No token/desktop; no DC traffic."
        },
        {
          "id": "disabled-account",
          "detector": "S",
          "condition": "Selected account disabled",
          "stopBoundary": "verify",
          "preserved": "No success result."
        },
        {
          "id": "deny-interactive",
          "detector": "A",
          "condition": "SeDenyInteractiveLogonRight applies despite valid password",
          "stopBoundary": "authorize",
          "preserved": "Credential verification remains historical; no successful console session."
        },
        {
          "id": "profile-failure",
          "detector": "P",
          "condition": "Profile startup fails after token creation",
          "stopBoundary": "desktop",
          "preserved": "Authentication history remains; desktopReady=false."
        }
      ],
      "acceptance": [
        "Every named actor/store is local; zero network messages in this profile.",
        "Token contains a synthetic local user SID, attributed group SIDs, privilege list with enabled flags, logon identifier and integrity label; no password or Kerberos ticket embedded.",
        "Credential-input buffers receive a declared cleanup event; durable verifier and token have different owners/lifetimes.",
        "No token exists at credential receipt or before authority/policy checks."
      ],
      "heldArtifacts": [
        "local account/verifier",
        "credential input buffer",
        "local policy",
        "validation result",
        "logon LUID",
        "primary token",
        "profile",
        "desktop session",
        "file DACL/decision"
      ],

    {
      "id": "WLOG02",
      "title": "Domain-member workstation: online AD DS password logon",
      "goal": "Connect local Windows sign-in to actual Kerberos AS/TGS work, local workstation service-ticket validation, and locally created access tokens.",
      "tier": "core",
      "actors": [
        "U: user",
        "L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider",
        "A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role",
        "P: user process/session and kernel token role",
        "K: AD DS KDC/account database",
        "M: workstation machine credential and local Kerberos acceptor"
      ],
      "preconditions": [
        "WORKSTATION is an ADDS member; CORP\\alice exists; DC/DNS/time and machine relationship work.",
        "Select AES password preauthentication; no NTLM fallback in this fixture; FAST disabled only to isolate WLOG06.",
        "Pin current supported Windows11 client, Server2025 KDC, policy and complete MS-KILE revision; logical roles are not separate external servers."
      ],
      "steps": [
        {
          "id": "input",
          "from": "U",
          "to": "L",
          "type": "local-input",
          "action": "Collect explicitly scoped CORP\\alice input and submit to the local Kerberos authentication package.",
          "artifacts": [
            "credential-input",
            "logon-request"
          ],
          "boundary": "LSASS submission is not a network request."
        },
        {
          "id": "as",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "K",
          "type": "network-exchange",
          "action": "Run existing AS request/reply model, including selected preauth metadata, client-derived key and KDC-owned authoritative key.",
          "artifacts": [
            "AS-REQ",
            "AS-REP",
            "user-account-key",
            "KDC-user-key",
            "opaque-TGT"
          ],
          "boundary": "No clear password crosses the KDC leg."
        },
        {
          "id": "as-accept",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "A",
          "type": "local-verify",
          "action": "Decrypt and validate the client part before acquiring the issued TGT session key and installing the opaque TGT.",
          "artifacts": [
            "accepted-TGT-credential"
          ],
          "boundary": "Ticket receipt is distinct from usable credential acquisition."
        },
        {
          "id": "host-ticket",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "K",
          "type": "network-exchange",
          "action": "Request host/workstation.corp.example for the workstation itself and validate its TGS reply.",
          "artifacts": [
            "host-TGS-REQ",
            "host-ticket",
            "host-session-key"
          ],
          "boundary": "Do not stop the sign-in explanation at receiving a TGT."
        },
        {
          "id": "local-ticket-check",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "M",
          "type": "local-call",
          "action": "The workstation Kerberos runtime interprets its host ticket and validated authorization data using its own service identity.",
          "artifacts": [
            "host-ticket",
            "validated-logon-information"
          ],
          "boundary": "This is local workstation processing, not a fabricated network AP exchange to another host."
        },
        {
          "id": "token",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "local-create",
          "action": "Combine validated domain identity/group information with local policy/alias membership and logon rights; create the primary token and start the session.",
          "artifacts": [
            "domain-SID",
            "group-SID-set",
            "local-policy",
            "primary-token",
            "desktop-session"
          ],
          "boundary": "Token issued locally, not sent by KDC."
        },
        {
          "id": "network-boundary",
          "from": "P",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "teaching-link",
          "action": "Offer a separate network-resource lesson using the retained credential context.",
          "artifacts": [
            "credential-context-reference"
          ],
          "boundary": "Desktop success does not authorize a share/file."
        }
      ],
      "negativeCases": [
        {
          "id": "wrong-password",
          "detector": "K",
          "condition": "Preauthentication fails",
          "stopBoundary": "as",
          "preserved": "No accepted user TGT or local token."
        },
        {
          "id": "clock-or-spn",
          "detector": "K/A",
          "condition": "Time or workstation service target invalid",
          "stopBoundary": "as or host-ticket",
          "preserved": "No invented local success; retain prior valid credential history where applicable."
        },
        {
          "id": "host-key-mismatch",
          "detector": "M",
          "condition": "Ticket cannot be accepted by the selected machine identity",
          "stopBoundary": "local-ticket-check",
          "preserved": "TGT receipt is not a desktop grant."
        },
        {
          "id": "denied-local-logon",
          "detector": "A",
          "condition": "Domain authentication succeeds but local deny right applies",
          "stopBoundary": "token",
          "preserved": "No usable desktop; no arbitrary cached bypass."
        },
        {
          "id": "password-change-required",
          "detector": "K",
          "condition": "Account requires change before authentication completes",
          "stopBoundary": "as",
          "preserved": "Explicit stop/cross-link; do not invent an inline password-change protocol."
        }
      ],
      "acceptance": [
        "Assert AS/TGS target, key owner, reply receipt/acceptance and local-token boundaries.",
        "No domain password transmitted to SAM, no SAM verifier masquerading as an AES key, and no user token copied out of a TGT.",
        "Token provenance lists domain identity/group facts separately from local aliases/privileges and application access decisions.",
        "Do not teach arbitrary Kerberos-error-to-NTLM fallback; a future compatibility branch needs its own sourced condition and carrier."
      ],
      "heldArtifacts": [
        "user/KDC AES handles",
        "AS client part/TGT/TGT key",
        "host ticket/key",
        "validated PAC/logon data",
        "local group/policy facts",
        "token",
        "profile/session"
      ],
      "crossLinks": [
        "Existing standalone ADDS/password lessons",
        "lab-smb-nonjoined-kerberos"
      ],

    {
      "id": "WLOG03",
      "title": "Domain member, explicit local account: same name, different SID",
      "goal": "Explain why .\\alice, WORKSTATION\\alice and CORP\\alice can select different authorities and do not become the same principal because their names match.",
      "tier": "core",
      "actors": [
        "U: user",
        "L: Winlogon/LogonUI and credential provider",
        "A: LSA/LSASS authentication and policy role",
        "P: user process/session and kernel token role",
        "S: local SAM authority",
        "K: ADDS authority shown as uncontacted"
      ],
      "preconditions": [
        "Machine is a domain member; both local alice and domain alice exist with deliberately different SIDs/password fixtures.",
        "Select .\\alice explicitly; no account-name guessing or silent authority fallback."
      ],
      "steps": [
        {
          "id": "scope",
          "from": "U",
          "to": "L",
          "type": "local-input",
          "action": "Choose the local account and show normalized authority WORKSTATION before submitting the password.",
          "artifacts": [
            "account-scope"
          ],
          "boundary": "Displayed name alone is not the identity."
        },
        {
          "id": "sam",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "S",
          "type": "local-call",
          "action": "Validate the local credential and read only local account/group information.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-verifier",
            "local-validation"
          ],
          "boundary": "KDC remains uncontacted."
        },
        {
          "id": "token",
          "from": "A",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "local-create",
          "action": "Authorize local logon and create a token with the machine-local SID.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-token"
          ],
          "boundary": "No CORP SID or domain TGT is inferred."
        },
        {
          "id": "compare",
          "from": "P",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "local-check",
          "action": "Run a selected local ACL check and show the different result for the hypothetical CORP SID without changing this process identity.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-ACL",
            "access-decision"
          ],
          "boundary": "Comparison does not transfer another principal token."
        },
        {
          "id": "network",
          "from": "P",
          "to": "P",
          "type": "teaching-link",
          "action": "Cross-link explicit domain network credentials while retaining this desktop identity.",
          "artifacts": [
            "local-token-reference"
          ],
          "boundary": "Network credential entry is a later independent action."
        }
      ],
      "negativeCases": [
        {
          "id": "domain-password-for-local-user",
          "detector": "S",
          "condition": "CORP password supplied for the selected local account",
          "stopBoundary": "sam",
          "preserved": "No fallback to CORP."
        },
        {
          "id": "local-account-missing",
          "detector": "S",
          "condition": "Selected local account absent",
          "stopBoundary": "sam",
          "preserved": "No fabricated domain logon."
        },
        {
          "id": "local-sid-denied",
          "detector": "P",
          "condition": "Local SID is absent from the selected allow ACL",
          "stopBoundary": "compare",
          "preserved": "Local logon stays successful."
        }
      ],
      "acceptance": [
        "Account-authority control is visible in beginner mode.",
        "Different SID values survive same-name fixtures and all replay modes.",
        "No DC/Kerberos/Netlogon message occurs in the selected local path."
      ],
      "heldArtifacts": [
        "normalized account authority",
        "local verifier",
        "local SID/token",
        "domain SID comparison metadata",
        "ACL decision"
